3500: Shallow water habitat use by young reef sharks has long been attributed to high food availability and low predation risk, facilitating rapid growth and survival. However, little is understood about the risk of predation within these areas. Using drone footage, two measures of predation risk (spatial overlap and encounter rate with predators) of young blacktip reef sharks, Carcharhinus melanopterus, and their reef predators (i.e., older conspecifics) were quantified in five terrestrial reef flats of Mo'orea, French Polynesia. Overall, we found little evidence of temporal partitioning of space as consistent measures of predation risk were observed across a diel cycle. While we found a consistent risk of predation across all surveyed sites, spatial overlap between young blacktips and their predators was greater in areas with high benthic habitat complexity. This was potentially due to an increase in shared food resources in complex habitats (i.e., teleost fish and crustaceans). Additionally, spatial overlap between young blacktips and their reef predators was disproportionate to the observed predator-prey encounter rates, indicating that external factors may limit the possible number of encounters from what would be expected by spatial overlap alone. We suggest that young blacktips remain in terrestrial reef flats despite regular interactions with predators through relying on their ability to out-manoeuvre their larger predators in these shallow complex environments.

3501: Essential habitats are areas which critically underpin the survival of species through one or multiple life stages. Although general habitat use has been broadly studied for tiger sharks, Galeocerdo cuvier, very little is understood about habitat use by neonate and young of the year sharks (YOY). Here, we aimed to identify essential habitats for juvenile tiger sharks, while assessing potential pupping grounds along the Queensland coast. We utilised multidecadal catch data from the shark control program to assess the prevalence of juveniles along the Queensland coast, and conducted targeted fishing surveys in the Palm and Whitsunday Islands. Cairns and Townsville regions had higher catches of juveniles relative to other locations on the coast. Research fishing surveys found a marked difference in juvenile (<2m TL) relative abundance between the Palm Islands (CPUE = 0.14 sharks per hook hours), and the Whitsundays at (CPUE = 0.0 sharks per hook hours). Acoustic tracking of sharks in the Palm Islands showed subadult/adult sharks (>2m TL) tended to have higher residency index, averaging at 0.0690, whereas smaller sharks (<2m TL) were much lower, at 0.0070. To date, Townsville and Cairns appear to be the most likely regions containing essential habitats for juvenile tiger sharks. To further explore this, additional targeted fishing surveys and tagging will be conducted over the next year in areas between Cairns and Townsville, including the Palm Island group.

3502: Fishing activities pose the primary threat to deepwater chondrichthyans (sharks, rays, and chimaeras). These species are highly susceptible to overexploitation but are frequently captured as bycatch. While international interest in understanding and reducing fishing mortality on chondrichthyans is growing, limited research has been conducted on deepwater species. In January 2024, at-vessel mortality and capture stress under normal fishing conditions were measured for deepwater chondrichthyans on Chatham Rise, New Zealand. At-vessel mortality and physical condition were assessed for 1301 unique specimens, representing 31 species and 15 families. A random subset of 247 specimens from 19 species were temporarily housed in an 800 L tank for up to 12h to monitor their health, evaluate capture stress and estimate short-term post-release mortality rates. A range of indicators related to physical (general condition and organ-specific examinations), behavioural (responses to stimuli and stress-related behaviours), and physiological status through blood analysis (blood-gas, acid-base, haematology, blood chemistry, and hormones) were collected. In total, 1627 physical and behavioural assessments were completed, and 471 blood samples collected. An overview of the sampling protocols, data collection, and future research plans will be presented.

3503: Understanding the behavioral responses of marine megafauna to anthropogenic disturbances is crucial for effective conservation management. To understand the effect of human aquatic recreation on manta ray behavior we employed aerial drone surveys to investigate the flight responses of reef manta rays (Mobula alfredi) in response to in-water human activity. Through coordinated UAS (drone) surveys conducted in a known manta ray habitat we analyzed the influence of human recreation choices on the flight responses of M. alfredi. Aerial drone technology offers a non-invasive approach, enabling the collection of high-resolution imagery and behavioral data over large spatial scales. The integration of drone technology in marine conservation strategies offers a promising avenue for assessing and mitigating human-induced impacts on marine megafauna. Preliminary findings suggest correlations between specific anthropogenic parameters and manta ray flight behaviors. These insights provide a foundation for developing management guidelines to protect M. alfredi populations while permitting ecotourism and aquatic recreation to coexist. Ultimately, this research contributes to the broader understanding of the ecological dynamics of reef manta rays and provides valuable tools for conservation practitioners to implement targeted management measures aimed at minimizing disturbance and ensuring the sustainable coexistence of M. alfredi with human activities in their natural habitats.

3504: The isiMangaliso Wetland Park is a large multi-use MPA along the east coast of South Africa. The area encompasses the southernmost coral reef systems of Africa and exhibits an extraordinarily high elasmobranch diversity. Due to its large size, the different management zonations within, and the presence of various habitats, the area represents a unique opportunity to investigate elasmobranch communities and the underlying factors governing their distributions and compositions. Furthermore, the marginal nature of the ecosystems necessitates a thorough understanding of local population dynamics and space use, as southward-expansions of population ranges are foreseeable due to climate change. The herein presented research project encompasses seasonality, diel shifts, MPA zonation, and the importance of habitat characteristics in shaping elasmobranch communities, with special focus on oceanographic features. Data is collected using BRUVs and a novel method of eDNA collection which aims to reduce replicate variability and increase detectability. As I am still in the early phase of my PhD, I have only sampled one season so far – two seasons by the time the conference takes place. Nonetheless, certain patterns are already manifesting, such as higher diversity/abundance near submarine canyons, reef structural complexity only playing a role for certain species, and the eDNA samples detecting species which have not yet been reported in the park.
3505: Ocean warming threatens all marine ecosystems with observed and predicted shifts in animal movements, range extensions, and changes in movement patterns documented across marine taxa. Understanding how threatened species, such as white sharks (Carcharodon carcharias), may respond to climate change contributes to the effective management and conservation of this vulnerable species. Ensuring that management approaches are responsive to changes in climate, species distributions, and habitat change can assist with the long-term survival of this species. Satellite Position Only Tags (SPOT) were deployed on 64 white sharks over 9-years (2015–2019) on the east coast of Australia from Forster to Lennox head, New South Whales. We used benthos type, bathymetry, and sea surface temperature to build a machine-learning resource selection function model to identify patterns in habitat selection and predict white shark occurrence in response to ocean warming. We determined that white sharks preferentially select sandy-bottomed habitats within 13 – 20 °C. While analysis is ongoing, our study will demonstrate the power of machine learning techniques to predict changes in habitat suitability and species distribution in the face of climate change.

3506: Environmental fluctuations can drive changes in animal behaviour, triggering annual migrations for food, optimal weather, or reproduction, as well as short-term activity changes. Using acoustic accelerometer tags deployed on over 600 white (Carcharodon carcharias) sharks from 2020 to 2024, we explored how environmental conditions (i.e., temperature, tides, moon phase and time of day) influence the activity of sharks in Eastern Australian waters. We identified that white sharks were more active between 1800 and 2400 at lower latitudes (-25 to -30 °S) and most active between 1000 and 1400 at higher latitudes (-40 °S). Wind direction was the primary factor driving white shark activity levels, with shark activity increasing in northwest winds likely due to calmer seas. In contrast, southeast winds, often associated with rougher seas, saw a decrease in white shark activity. This study will be used to inform shark management programs and the public of environmental factors that increase white shark activity and certain times of day, locations, and environmental conditions that may increase the risk of shark encounters.

3507: Along the coast of south-eastern Australia, ocean temperatures are increasing at a rapid rate, but our understanding of temperate elasmobranch shifts in distributions and abundance in relation to these environmental changes is limited, and the extent to which marine protected areas (MPAs) offer protection is lacking. This research, located along Victoria, Australia, aimed to investigate habitat and environmental associations to predict elasmobranch species distributions and abundance now and into the future and determine the effectiveness of MPAs on protecting populations of elasmobranchs under current and future environmental conditions. Using a dataset of 1,048 baited remote underwater video stations (BRUVS), observations of six elasmobranch species abundances and elasmobranch richness, we developed generalised additive models (GAMs) to associate those observations with environmental drivers including satellite and model derived oceanographic variables and seafloor habitat. We found SST and wave energy to be the main environmental drivers of abundance and that future changes in those variables were likely to drive decreases in populations of 45 – 75% and MPAs protect varying levels of predicted populations with proportional protection increasing into the future.

3508: Shark ecotourism is a non-extractive alternative to fishing with capacity to generate revenue, offer employment, and support conservation. Little is known about the spatial ecology of common coastal sharks in Hawaiʻi, even the most abundant species encountered at Oʻahu ecotourism sites. I am investigating how these shark populations are responding to the growing number of ecotourism operations (2 in 2007; >15 in 2023) by assessing historical (2007-2018) and contemporary (2019-2023) movements, residency and abundance of sharks associated with these sites. From 2019-2023, I tagged 38 Galapagos, sandbar and tiger sharks at ecotourism sites to compare their movements with 47 sharks tagged at these sites from 2007-2009;2014. Preliminary analyses show sharks captured at ecotourism sites visit these sites regularly but range widely around Oʻahu and beyond. These ecotour-tagged sharks show clear diel behavior patterns, associating with moorings by day, roaming further afield at night. There is evidence of contiguous seasonal migrations by sharks in the number of sharks detected at ecotourism sites. 53 sharks tagged at distant locations were detected at ecotourism sites occasionally passed through the area remaining for a few minutes or a few days. Analyses are ongoing to determine whether shark residency is increasing over time at these sites. This data will fill key knowledge gaps about shark ecology. These results will facilitate science driven management of shark ecotourism.

3509: Most ecological studies focus on top predators and their influences on lower trophic levels or on basal primary producers that structure marine ecosystems. Mesopredators receive less attention but outnumber top predators in both biomass and number of species, and play essentials roles in linking upper and lower trophic levels. Shifts in ecosystems dynamics, partly driven by changing climates and declines in the abundance of top marine predators might lead to mesopredators becoming more prevalent and to broadening their trophic role due to increased competition. Characterisation of niche width and overlap can help better understand resource use, whereby narrow and wide niche width can be indicative of specialist or generalist feeding, respectively. Niche overlap can be an indicator of shared resources or competition. Here, I use fatty acids and stable isotopes to inform diet and calculate niche width and overlap of 16 sympatric Chondrichthyes to estimate resource sharing and identify generalist and specialist feeders. Muscle fatty acids revealed significant differences in diet between all species, and grouping into three distinct clusters; pelagic feeders, reef-demersal feeders, and deep-demersal feeders. It is imperative to understand resource partitioning as there is a growing concern that due to declining top-predator abundance and subsequent mesopredator release, the trophic roles of chondrichthyan mesopredators will shift, changing food web structure along with it.
3510: Acoustic telemetry often involves an invasive method of internal tagging, wherein the animal is incised, a transmitter internally inserted into the coelomic cavity, after which the incision is closed with sutures to aid wound closure, healing, and tag retention. However, the stitching of the wound can be time-consuming especially when field conditions are not optimal, leading to additional handling stress, which can be fatal in sensitive species or extreme cases. We assessed whether animal welfare of internally-tagged sharks can be improved by reducing handling time through keeping incision wounds unsutured. A 63-day captive study measured physical (i.e., macroscopic assessment of incision healing progress), bacterial dynamics (i.e., colony forming units), physiological (i.e., cortisol levels), and histological (i.e., cell type and morphology) responses to two internal acoustic transmitter tagging procedures (i.e., with and without sutures) in twelve Port Jackson (Heterodontus portusjacksoni) sharks. Sutures facilitated fast wound closure but led to greater inflammation compared to unsutured incisions. Sutured incisions also had ~100 times more colony forming units present than unsutured incisions, despite the use of autoclaved surgical tools. Tag retention was 100% in both treatments and incisions were, on average, completely healed by ~14 days, but unsutured incisions healed slower. Our study contributes to our understanding of elasmobranch healing and tagging effects.

3511: Marine animals rely on their epidermal microbiomes (resident communities of bacteria and viruses) to eliminate pathogens and avoid infection. The virome, comprised of viruses and bacteriophages, is critical to marine epidermal microbiome defense systems. Sharks demonstrate a unique resistance to epidermal infections despite frequent injury and exposure to opportunistic pathogens. Shark epidermal immunity stems in part from innate mechanisms, such as skin morphology, immune responses, and antimicrobial secretions, but the role of the epidermal virome in shark health is an outstanding question. We sampled the epidermis of sharks from the southwestern Pacific, including white (Carcharodon carcharias), tiger (Galeocerdo cuvier), dusky (Carcharhinus obscurus), and sandbar (Carcharhinus plumbeus) sharks (total n=43). Some individuals had epidermal lesions at various healing stages (n=5), which were sampled along with nearby undamaged skin. Viral abundance was estimated using flow cytometry. Wounded skin harbored over 10-fold higher abundance of virus-like particles (VLPs) compared to undamaged skin on the same individual, and higher VLP abundance than undamaged conspecifics. To investigate this phenomenon experimentally, epidermal viral abundance was estimated on captive Port Jackson sharks (Heterodontus portusjacksoni, n=10) with healing surgical wounds, sampled prior to incision and at 7-day intervals for 21 days post-incision. Here we present the results of that experiment.

3512: Vertebrate cartilage possesses limited regenerative abilities in responding to injuries and degeneration due to sudden and/or extreme load exposure as well as medical conditions such as arthritis. Extreme loads are borne by chondrichthyan fishes thriving in environments from shallow water (< 200m) to deep water (> 200m) of up to 3,000m. While many extant species live at these depths or migrate between different zones of the water column, the mechanisms they have evolved to withstand and adapt to constant and/or varying hydrostatic pressures are unknown. To investigate whether any key biological adaptations to constant/varying extreme hydrostatic pressures are present, this study assesses two skeletal regions (cranium and vertebra) across four devil ray species (n = 2) that show frequent vertical movements. Preliminary results are compared with five deepwater chondrichthyan species (n = 2) that never (or only seasonally) surface. Using a multi-scale approach, the research aims to characterise 1) the histological organisation, composition, and architecture of un-mineralised and mineralised cartilage and 2) the mechanical properties of these tissues and their interfaces. This comparative approach will help to build a baseline knowledge of the composition and arrangement of cartilage and extracellular matrix that has naturally evolved to withstand high hydrostatic pressures and will inform future research in cartilage tissue engineering, regenerative medicine, and biomimetics.

3513: Animal aggregations are common and often driven by resource availability and synchrony of daily or seasonal activity. However, information on aggregation ecology is limited for many species, including the white shark (Carcharodon carcharias), where the Neptune Islands is one of Australia's largest shark aggregation sites. Non-random associations of four communities suggest that factors other than prey abundance might influence aggregatory patterns. This study aimed to determine whether the co-occurrence of individual sharks, and variation in visitation patterns, is influenced by relatedness, a known driver of aggregation in other animal systems. To achieve this, 133 white sharks were genotyped at 5,000 SNP loci using reduced genome representation sequencing. Relatedness amongst shark pairs was determined using a combination of co-ancestry coefficients and likelihood approaches, and tests for correlations between shark relatedness and location, degree of residency and seasonality were conducted. Analyses indicated low levels of relatedness among pairs and no significant relationship between genetic relatedness and location, degree of residency or seasonality of shark visitation. This study shows that relatedness is not likely to be a factor influencing visitation and shark co-occurrence, highlighting the need for further research to identifying alternative drivers of aggregatory patterns at the Neptune Islands to help inform future management of this key marine predator.

3514: Our understanding of the trophic role of elasmobranchs is often limited and can be attributed to the difficulty in obtaining sufficient sample sizes and material. Tissues alongside jaws are often stored in a range of chemical preservatives or frozen for long-term keepsake or to reach a desired appearance by researchers, museums or private collectors. If we are to use preserved jaws for dietary studies, we must first understand the impacts jaw preservation methods have on carbon, nitrogen and sulphur stable isotopes of elasmobranch teeth. This remains a major limitation, curtailing the use samples from museum and private collections. We assessed if chemical preservation affected tooth stable isotopes of three different elasmobranch species when freshly preserved, or after six months, and if this impact varies among different tooth morphologies. Findings showed that there was no impact of preservation on tooth stable isotopes. Impact on the biochemistry of the tooth samples was also noted to be potentially affected by the amount of tissue processed and analysed. Ongoing sample processing and analysis aims to provide further explanations to the variability seen in the preliminary findings. By understanding how preservation impacts stable isotopes of elasmobranch teeth, preserved jaws from museum or private collections will become available and complement samples from fresh jaws to study the trophic ecology of elasmobranchs.

3515: The Slender Bambooshark (Chiloscyllium indicum) is a common Indo-West Pacific species at risk from increasing fishing pressure and coastal development. Though wide ranging within the region, little is known about the ecology of this small mesopredator. We tagged 10 sharks with acoustic transmitters to investigate movement within an area in the Johor Strait between Singapore and Malaysia. Preliminary results indicate that at this site these small, benthic, sharks exhibit diel patterns of movement from deeper areas within a shipping channel, to shallower coastal areas. Tracking data of up to 400+ days for some individuals indicates that home-ranges are small. While this may mean that populations are particularly vulnerable to human impacts at a local scale, conversely it also suggests that spatial management of relatively small areas could be a valuable approach to protecting this vulnerable species.
3516: Many elasmobranchs, including shark-like rays, play a complex role in maintaining the balance in marine food webs. They prey on a wide range of marine organisms and occupy a range of apex and meso-predatory roles that maintain the stability of marine food webs. Thus, Information regarding the diet of elasmobranchs is important to understand their natural history, role, and function in marine ecosystems. This study aims to investigate Critically Endangered Wedgefish (Rhynchobatus spp.) diet in the Indo-West Pacific region based on geography, seasonal pattern, size, and sex class. To date, data collection from Southwest Aceh and Northern Java, Indonesia, between October 2023 and February 2024, consists of 47 individuals from three species (R. australiae, R. laevis and R. springeri show wedgefish diet items, including Mollusca (Class Cephalopoda and Bivalvia), Crustacea (Order Decapoda and Infraorder Brachyura), Teleostei (Family Ballistidae, Mullidae, Genus Namipterus and Priyacantus tayenus). Further step to acquire more accurate results include using environmental DNA analysis that have become increasingly popular as a sensitive, non-invasive technique for dietary assessments.

3517: Large predatory elasmobranchs are vital components of marine ecosystems, largely via top-down control of meso-predator and prey abundance and presence. The tiger shark, Galeocerdo cuvier, is one of a few larger elasmobranch species along the eastern Australian coast fulfilling this top tier role. The large-scale movement of individuals plays an important role in trophic links connecting distant and distinct coastal and pelagic ecosystems. Despite this there are some glaring gaps in species' ecological and biological knowledge in published data resulting from a lack of adult male tiger sharks in movement analysis and subsequent conclusions. From targeted capture and deployment of satellite tags onto adult male tiger sharks, male-specific movement has been captured. Here we show that as with other animals, tiger sharks exhibit sex-biased movement that may play a major role in survival strategies and biological functions. While juveniles and adult female tiger sharks exhibit distinct trends in migration times and fine-scale diel movement, adult males are potentially utilizing different pathways and cues for movement and behaviour. While previously presumed, the implications of identifying sex-related movement allows for further analysis that may provide insight into biological and ecological interactions, such as location of mating grounds or indirect versus direct pressure among ecosystems.

3518: The pyjama shark is a Scyliorhinid species endemic to South Africa. Even though it is kept in captivity in many aquaria, there is a lack of research on its growth and development. In this study, we investigated the fertilization rate of eggs and the age at female sexual maturation in captive sharks and compared their growth to that of wild individuals. This is the first study to compare the growth of captive and wild catsharks as well as the first study to compare growth in male and female pyjama sharks. The mean incubation rate (±standard error of the mean [SE]) was 239.46 ± 4.97 days, the mean Lt of hatchlings (±SE) was 14.65 ± 0.24 cm, and the mean Wt (±SE) was 17.19 ± 0.75 g. One female laid fertilized eggs 6.6 years after hatching and was considered sexually mature. Both in captivity and in the wild, males showed negative allometric growth and females showed isometric growth. The growth performance (Φ') was also greater in captive sharks compared to wild sharks regardless of sex. However, there was significant variation in growth between individuals of the same sex. The similar growth patterns found in wild and captive populations are a very useful tool for informing future conservation management if the population of this shark species were to decline in the future and also prove that captive studies for this species are transferable to wild populations with regard to sexual differences.

3519: Noise pollution in the ocean has been increasing by nearly three decibels every ten years, causing a disruption in a previously serene acoustic environment. The Australian ghost shark, Callorhinchus milii, migrates from great depths to reproduce in shallow waters and is predicted to rely heavily on its hearing, as indicated by the size and unique specialisations of its ears. We aim to determine the possible impacts of anthropogenic noise on the development of the auditory system of C. milii. Captive embryos were exposed during their entire development to two acoustic conditions: an ambient soundscape or boat noise. Embryos and hatchlings were collected at different timepoints, preserved and scanned using micro-computed tomography. The nervous system, including the morphology of the hearing apparatus and the brain, will be compared between treatments by quantifying the volume, size and shape of the inner ear compared to controls throughout development. This is the first study investigating the impact of noise on the development of any chondrichthyan species. Our research will establish, for the first time, an overlooked but potentially severe threat to an important group of cartilaginous fishes.

3520: Reef sharks have experienced widespread declines across much of the world's coral reefs as a result of decades of overexploitation. Large knowledge gaps concerning the abundance of reef sharks worldwide have limited effective restoration and management of coastal shark populations. Although recent research has assessed the global status and conservation potential of reef sharks, causal questions remain regarding the effects of current management strategies. Using data from baited remote underwater video systems (BRUVS) from 371 sampling locations across 58 nations globally, we implemented a causal inference framework to determine cause-and-effect relationships between direct management actions and reef shark abundance. We developed Bayesian hierarchical models comprised of regional, national, reef, and set spatial scales to quantify the effect of shark sanctuaries, marine protected areas, and fishing restrictions on the relative abundance of reef sharks. Counterfactual scenarios in which different management interventions are implemented at each reef were used to determine the net benefit of management actions at the national level based on expected changes in shark abundance and the likelihood of management action. Here, we highlight the power of causal inference in understanding ecological relationships beyond the capabilities of predictive techniques typically used with observational data and evaluate management-related drivers of global reef shark abundance.

3521: As most people will not encounter sharks in the wild, the media's portrayal of these animals contributes to public perception and conservation support. Therefore, understanding how sharks are portrayed in the media is important for shark conservation research. This poster presents findings from various studies exploring sharks in the media and the impact of media portrayals on public perception. Through analysing 2,643 shark-related Facebook posts made by Australian news media outlets during 2016 it was found that 87% of all the news-related Facebook pages published at least one post related to sharks and only 49 days in 2016 had no published shark-related posts. Through analysing 109 shark films it was found that almost all of these films (96%) overtly portrayed shark-human interactions as being potentially threatening to humans and only one film did not include potentially threatening interactions. Further, when investigating animal related horror films more broadly, sharks were found to be the most depicted animal. To begin to understand the impact of these portrayals, a mixed-method experiment found that people's perception of risk of sharks significantly increased after viewing shark related news headlines. Since public perception of shark mitigation can motivate politicians to fund and support shark management and conservation, it is important that research continues to explore the impact of media portrayal of sharks and peoples' fear and acceptance of sharks broadly.
3522: Shark vertebrae are biogeochemical archives of environmental conditions and are proving to be a valuable tool in determining life history traits. We here investigate the use and inter-complementary of high spatial resolution spectroscopy, X-Ray spectrometry and mass-spectrometry techniques to unravel the sclerochronological life records. Thin sections of four elasmobranch species were examined through a range of instruments including Raman, μXRF, LA-ICP-MS, and high-resolution SIMS (SHRIMP). High-definition maps and transect analyses were amalgamated to produce interpretable, reliable data images. Through Raman spectroscopy the nature of cartilage crystallisation to bioapatite was captured, allowing the nature of sequential modelling of the vertebra to be analysed. Elemental maps (μXRF, LA-ICP-MS) provided insights into the concentrations of minor and trace elements capturing patterns of seasonality within the chronological structure. These maps may provide more accurate ways to age sharks, particularly for species that are notoriously difficult to age. 3523: Current elasmobranch ageing methods often leave sharks systematically underaged, having severe management implications, and impacting demographic analysis and estimation of population recovery rates. Validating ageing techniques and enhancing our ability to infer habitat use across ages is fundamental to proper management. The growth mechanisms of shark vertebrae and the incorporation of trace elements (and their isotopic signatures) into the internal structure of vertebrae are poorly understood. Further, the extent of the information that can be gathered by analysing trace elements along the growth axis of vertebrae is still developing. To find a more reliable ageing technique that removes ambiguity and seeks to validate conventional methods (optical microscopy), vertebrae from pelagic, coastal and riverine species have been selected and analysed to discriminate the presence of elemental variations in their vertebrae using SEM-EDS, EPMA, μXRF, LA-ICP-MS and LA-MC-ICP-MS. It was found that elemental distribution varied significantly between species from different habitat types, and variances were more pronounced in coastal and riverine species that are exposed to terrigenous runoff. We find that μXRF effectively improved the visibility of ageing structures, and expressed patterns based on seasonality, further supported by radiogenic Sr isotopic ratios (87Sr/86Sr by LA-MC-ICP-MS) and may prove a more accurate way to age sharks.

3524: The nocturnal ecology of elasmobranchs has often been overlooked due to the logistical challenges of conducting nocturnal surveys. 3525: Tiger sharks are wide-ranging predators that remain resident to specific areas seasonally in the South Pacific Ocean, presumably due to factors associated with foraging, reproduction, physiology, or a combination thereof. The contribution of these factors towards movement decisions is not well understood — knowledge of which can help identify potential impacts from changing environmental conditions or manage human-shark interactions. Our study explores the relative importance of abiotic factors affecting the movements of tiger sharks from a relatively small-scale during summer aggregations at Norfolk Island, Australia, to their expansive movements across the western South Pacific. Sharks were tracked with either acoustic (n = 42 individuals) or satellite (n = 35 individuals) telemetry between 2020 and 2023. Movements around Norfolk Island were focused on the west side of the island, likely in response to a known scavenging site associated with butcher waste disposal or to a wedge-tailed shearwater colony. At a larger scale, habitat suitability modelling indicated that distance from the nearest land was the most important variable with some influence of sea surface temperature and bathymetry, but independent of chlorophyll levels and bathymetrical slope, across all months of the year. Both small- and large-scale findings highlight reliance on being close to land throughout their movements, potentially as a method to optimise access to food sources originating from land.

3526: The millions of data that have been collected on the movement and space use of sharks and rays worldwide have been crucial in advancing knowledge of the complex interactions that occur within aquatic ecosystems and have helped identify critical conservation gaps and facilitate effective management strategies. Nevertheless, research output across studies, systems, or even species are often not readily findable, accessible, interoperable, or reusable (FAIR) hindering the prioritisation and optimisation of research and management impact. Here, we introduce TrackdAT, an open-source online portal that hosts metadata from over 2500 peer-reviewed acoustic telemetry articles worldwide. Using TrackdAT, we highlight >350 studies tracking >100 species of sharks and rays and summarize common trends in study topics, objectives, findings, and overall impact. Furthermore, we explore spatial and temporal patterns in shark and ray tracking research in Oceania and globally. We illustrate how acoustic telemetry research has broadened our ecological knowledge of species interactions, critical habitats, timing and spatial extent of movements, ontogenetic shifts, and spawning behaviour of chondrichthyans. We also demonstrate the utility of TrackdAT for identifying gaps in existing research, mobilizing knowledge at regional and global scales, encouraging stakeholder engagement, and optimizing the future of tracking research for sharks and rays.

3527: Sharks and rays are increasingly threatened due to overexploitation, prompting international conservation efforts such as species and genus-specific listings on Appendix II of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES). We investigated the discrepancies between reported catch data for CITES-listed shark species from publicly available databases for catches and international trade. We found substantial disparities between reported catches and documented trade of CITES-listed shark species. Factors contributing to these discrepancies may include inadequate monitoring and reporting mechanisms, misclassifications of species, low levels of data resolution, and lack of communication and cohesiveness between international bodies' databases. Understanding the root causes of these discrepancies is crucial for effective conservation and fisheries management. Improved collaboration and data sharing between bodies monitoring catch, particularly in Areas Beyond National Jurisdiction (ABNJs) and CITES will enhance the accuracy of information on shark catch and trade, enabling more informed conservation policies and enforcement measures. 3528: Globally, whale shark (Rhincodon typus) conservation is guided by research at aggregation sites. 3529: The Queensland SharkSmart drone trial was established in September 2020 to investigate the effectiveness of drones as a shark bite mitigation tool in Queensland conditions. Highest sighting rates have occurred at North Stradbroke Island and Burleigh Beach on the Gold Coast, with lowest sightings at Alexandra Headland Beach on the Sunshine Coast. 3530: Zooplankton are important in ocean ecosystems as they link primary productivity to higher trophic levels. Large planktivores such as reef manta rays (Mobula alfredi) rely on zooplankton productivity hotspots to meet their energetic requirements, and often aggregate at predictable locations. Certain acoustic Doppler current profilers (ADCP) have the capacity to undertake sustained (3 months) high vertical resolution (3mm) biological surveys using the integrated wideband echosounder. In this study, hydrodynamic conditions that lead to foraging events were investigated using data collected by bed-mounted, upwards-facing Nortek Signature ADCP deployed in Hanifaru Bay, the Maldives. These localised datasets that link the hydrodynamic mechanisms responsible for plankton accumulation to the foraging landscape of M. alfredi will help to understand the mechanisms that link predator-prey interactions to the properties of the habitat. 3531: Reef manta rays (Mobula alfredi) are a K-selected species characterized by low reproductive potential with long gestation times and live births to single pups at a time. Their life-history traits make them vulnerable to anthropogenic pressures, and populations are classified as vulnerable to extinction. Yet, reproductive patterns and associated habitats are still poorly understood. Here, the Project Manta photo ID database was examined to study reproductive patterns of M. alfredi on Australia's east coast. Between 2007 and 2021, 8280 sightings of 1592 individuals were recorded between Saunders Reef (11.30°S) and South West Rocks (30.9°S). 301 pregnancies among 762 females were recorded. Noticeably, some females were reported pregnant in consecutive years, although resting periods varied among individuals. Pregnancies recorded around Lady Elliot Island (LEI) and North Stradbroke Island (NSI) broadly followed temporal patterns, with pregnant individuals commonly sighted at LEI in late June before moving to NSI during Austral summer to give birth. These are preliminary results as data are currently being analysed. Moving forward, this research aims to establish a standardized framework in collaboration with the Okinawa Churaumi Aquarium. By identifying visual cues of each pregnancy stage, this study will provide recommendations to minimize observer bias and maximize the effective use of photo IDs for future databases.

3532: Intertidal flats provide high-value nursery grounds for juvenile rays, and where multiple species exist in these environments, they commonly partition prey resources and occupy different niche spaces. Thus, examining foraging strategies at the species level is meaningful for identifying key prey resources and understanding how patterns vary by ecological context. In this study, I assessed the diets of sympatric whiprays, H. australis, and M. toshi, at two intertidal sandflats in N QLD (Blacksoil Creek and Lucinda Beach). My objectives were to describe dietary consumption and overlap of these species during early life stages and compare patterns between sites. Gastric lavage was used to obtain stomach content samples for both species in Nov. 2023-2024 (n = 71). Across sites, both whiprays had strong preferences for decapod crustaceans over other benthic prey, but H. australis had a broader dietary niche than M. toshi. At Blacksoil Creek, H. australis consumed more soldier crabs and Callianassid shrimp than at Lucinda Beach. An absence of these prey types for M. toshi created further dietary distinction. Prey selection for M. toshi was similar across sites, where they specialised on surface-dwelling shrimps. Results suggested there may also be differences by size for H. australis, which can be explored further. Overall, comparing dietary habits among elasmobranch species and across different habitats will improve our understanding on their foraging ecology in intertidal zones.
3533: Conservation of threatened stingrays relies on taxonomic clarity and the accurate knowledge of a species' spatial ecology. Photo identification (photo-ID) and citizen science can aid in accumulating large datasets to study both spatial ecology and taxonomy. We used photo-ID, citizen science, and AI to clarify the distribution of Taeniura lymma and Taeniura lessoni, examine the effectiveness of citizen science data in spatial ecology research, and explore the potential of AI in distinguishing between closely related species. Images and associated metadata were collected from online image-sharing platforms, researcher-directed surveys, and a dedicated citizen science program. Images were masked, augmented, and used to train and evaluate the deep-learning AI models. Citizen science imagery revealed that T. lymma occurs across the Indian and Indo-Pacific oceans, while T. lessoni occurs along the eastern and western outskirts of T. lymma's range, suggesting possible patterns of origin and speciation through dispersal. Furthermore, the deep-learning model successfully identified T. lymma and T. lessoni with high accuracy (86.7%) and precision (83.7%), despite being trained on a small dataset (179 images). These results contribute new data on taxonomic distribution of closely-related rays, demonstrating the value of citizen science in spatial ecology research, and provide a crucial first step into further applications of innovative technology for stingray spatial ecology.

3534: Predator-prey dynamics profoundly influence ecosystem trophic ecology. Killer whales (Orcinus orca), are cosmopolitan apex predators, attracting ongoing media and research attention for their selective consumption of shark livers, notably those of white sharks (Carcharodon carcharias). Beyond recent events, killer whales exhibit a striking pattern of targeting specific tissue types in over 32 marine species, encompassing brain, tongue, livers, intestines, and eggs. This selective behaviour, coupled with their unmatched intelligence and observed dexterity, suggests drivers beyond mere prey availability and catchability. While this behaviour has been attributed to the nutritional content of specific tissues, this has never been investigated. Here we use approximately 500 samples, comparing targeted and non-targeted prey tissue type. Our preliminary results demonstrate significant differences in calorie content across taxa and between targeted and untargeted tissue types. Furthermore, fatty acid profiles differentiated between untargeted and targeted prey, primarily driven by non-essential fatty acids. These findings indicate that nutritional content contributes to shaping the picky eating habits of killer whales globally. These findings offer new insights into the factors influencing extreme feeding behaviours in predators, highlighting the necessity for ongoing research to understand the drivers and consequences of this behaviour.

3535: Coastal marine environments are highly productive and complex ecosystems that support many elasmobranch species due to the abundance of shelter and prey, which increases their susceptibility to environmental (e.g. temperature, waves, freshwater input) and anthropogenic (wastewater, pollution) changes compared to pelagic ecosystems. The abundance and diversity of elasmobranch species also leads to co-occurring communities of sharks and rays, where species must partition resources to avoid competitive exclusion. We determined the resource use of two South Australian mesopredators, Port Jackson sharks and southern eagle rays, using trophic and spatial niche quantification via fatty acid and stable isotope analysis and acoustic telemetry. Port Jackson sharks exhibited seasonal site fidelity, moving to more productive, estuarine environments during winter and returning to their tagging location in summer. Southern eagle rays demonstrated high, year-round site fidelity to the area they were tagged, with no seasonal changes in residency. These different patterns of site fidelity caused minimal overlap in space use between the species, suggesting this might be an important factor facilitating coexistence. Quantifying these patterns of resource use and overlap is necessary to determine species' resilience to habitat shifts and fluctuating prey availability resulting from environmental change or anthropogenic activities.

3536: The critically endangered Maugean skate only survives in Macquarie Harbour, southwest Tasmania. 3537: Elasmobranchs play a key role in the marine ecosystem that faces many threats from human activity. Anthropogenic sound is now recognised as a global pollutant, but the effects on sharks are poorly understood. Using a behavioural playback laboratory experiment, we exposed adult Port Jackson sharks (Heterodontus portusjacksoni) to biological and anthropogenic sounds. Sharks were exposed to two acoustic conditions containing ambient or boat sounds in a 'before – during – after' exposure experiment. Behaviours included swimming activity, tracking distance from the sound-source, use of a shelter structure, and respiration rate. While no significant differences were observed across their activities during treatment phases of playback, Port Jackson sharks showed an increased use of the shelter during boat playback versus ambient, and an increase in respiratory rate in the during phase of boat playback that was not observed in ambient trials. In the after phase of exposure to boat sounds, we found an increase in inactivity, coupled with a decrease in respiratory rate. These findings suggest that there is a complex relationship between physiological and behavioural impacts to sound that requires further research efforts. We demonstrate that anthropogenic sound affects H. portusjacksoni but may not be determined through measuring behaviour alone. Future research should include additional physiological measures to assess the overall impact of anthropogenic sounds on elasmobranchs.
3538: With many shark and ray populations in decline owing to overfishing, international action including through the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES), is taking shape for a growing number of species. A lack of management ensuring sustainability and Illegal activity are core reasons for their depletion. There is national, regional and global action to resolve this issue through a range of domestic regulations, regional/international agreements, industry and eco-standards and consumer-led campaigns. Underlying the success of all these is the need to demonstrate provenance of shark products to sustainable and legal sources. At the moment, there is no trade-based mechanism to distinguish between shark products derived from legal or illegal sources. SharkTrace (https://www.traffic.org/sharktrace/) was developed as an important step in in the process of monitoring and surveillance of species-specific trade quotas are documentation systems that trace shark products from point of capture to the point of export. Designed to verify product sources and legality, the SharkTrace system is comprised of an overarching webserver database that integrates information from mobile applications on the fishing vessel, transport vehicles and processing facilities. The "Vessel" application is used to record and "tag" the shark catch and any processing that occurs onboard the fishing vessel out at sea before landing. The "On the road" can monitor catch movements from the vessel unload to and from multiple receivers, while the "Factory" application is used to record reprocessing and repacking of landed catch information.

3540: Most of the world is covered in ocean, meaning fisheries management is required for over 70% of the world's surface. 3541: Cartilaginous fishes use electroreception and mechanoreception for orientation and feeding at close range. Pore distribution and abundance were assessed via digital mapping of the two sensory pore types and their corresponding canals. DiceCT imaging was used to accurately map the ampullary system and confirm the size and position of ampullary clusters, and the length and orientation of canals. 3542: Shark populations can be susceptible to overexploitation from fishing due to their conservative life histories that result in overall low biological productivity. Accurate species-specific data is needed to monitor changes in population dynamics. Age estimates, for example, provide the basis for other demographic parameters such as growth, maturity, and mortality. 3545: Sharks, rays, and chimaeras (hereafter ‘sharks’) are often overlooked in spatial planning for biodiversity conservation. The initiative identifies three-dimensional portions of habitat that are important for one or more shark species and have the potential to be managed for conservation. A set of science-based criteria are used to delineate these areas and consider species vulnerability, range restriction, life-history (reproduction, feeding, resting, movement, undefined aggregations), and special attributes (distinctiveness, diversity). These criteria are being applied to all environments where sharks occur across 13 ISRA regions covering the entire globe. Collaboration is paramount with experts convening at regional workshops to share information and propose important areas. Sixty five ISRAs have been delineated in the Central and South American Pacific and 75 proposals are undergoing review for the Mediterranean and Black Seas. Areas are also currently being evaluated for the Western Indian Ocean and other regions will follow. Peer-reviewed and approved ISRAs are mapped and added to a publicly available eAtlas (www.sharkrayareas.org). By centralising key information on shark habitat use and behaviour, ISRAs provide a foundation to ensure sharks are included in area-based management. This assists governments and policymakers in meeting global biodiversity and conservation targets, especially when such areas are overlapped with other approaches such as Important Marine Mammal Areas (IMMAs). Results from the ISRA initiative will support shark conservation by increasing information available when considering spatial management of these highly threatened species.

3546: Large sharks are important predators in marine ecosystems, influencing the overall functioning of ecosystems and the trophic connectivity between different regions (Heithaus et al., 2008; Estes et al., 2011). However, they face intense fishing pressure, particularly in coastal areas that serve as nurseries for many juvenile sharks (Fowler et al., 2005; Heupel et al., 2007). Understanding the spatial and temporal ecology of sharks in interaction with fisheries, especially in coastal ecosystems such as estuaries and lagoons, is crucial for their conservation. Many shark species, including Sphyrna lewini (scalloped hammerhead shark) and Carcharhinus limbatus (blacktip shark), are considered threatened with extinction (Dulvy et al., 2014). Recent observations in artisanal fishing in Gabon have revealed an abundance of juvenile sharks belonging to these two species, suggesting the presence of undocumented nurseries. The southern coast of Gabon, with its lagoon complexes and mangrove habitats, could play a key role in maintaining shark populations in the equatorial Atlantic (Cadenat et al., 1955; Mourier et al., 2013). This study aims to demonstrate the existence of nurseries for Sphyrna lewini and Carcharhinus limbatus in Gabon by studying captures, the maturity of captured individuals, and their trophic ecology.
Session 1: Insights into the spatial ecology of elasmobranch fish
3547: Over one third of elasmobranch species are threatened with extinction with nearly all species impacted by fisheries, typically from bycatch. While much research has been conducted on the impacts of certain threats on elasmobranchs, i.e., fishing, climate, discarding, and finning, there is a gap in the knowledge of how elasmobranch distributions might respond to population decline as a result of these threats. Furthermore, not all species will recover at the same rate, as some species are intrinsically more sensitive than others. Our goal was to determine the sensitivity of local elasmobranch species and highlight areas where these species and threats consistently overlap. Here we have determined the biological sensitivity of 44 species of elasmobranch found in Irish waters using the metric rmax, the maximum intrinsic rate of population increase. Oviparous species were found to have higher rmax than than ovoviviparous species in general, and the deep sea species had the lowest rmax, determining these species to be the most sensitive. Next we applied a species distribution modelling (SDM) approach to predict the distribution of 3 sensitive elasmobranch species found in Irish waters, as determined by rmax. Projections identified a change in the spatial distribution and extent of several species, with the results used to identify potential ‘hotspots’ of sensitive elasmobranchs in Irish waters based on intrinsic and extrinsic factors. Outputs of this work will help to improve the understanding of the local variability of elasmobranch species and provide support to expand and improve the management of protected areas and species.

3548: Skates (Rajidae) are important commercial species around the British Isles, yet there is currently limited information to aid the identification of potentially important habitats, such as spawning and nursery grounds. The neonates and juveniles of skate species have been recorded in scientific trawl surveys, with juveniles of most species proportionally more frequent in beam trawl surveys than in otter trawl surveys. The Great Eggcase Hunt is a long-standing (2003 to present) citizen science recording project that collates georeferenced data for elasmobranch eggcases, primarily from around the British Isles. This provided verified species-specific data for a total of 227,407 specimens from 11 skate species. Purse Search Ireland provided a further 2,491 records of 10 skate species. Eggcases from the genus Raja were the most frequently observed skate eggcases from much of the British coastline, and juveniles were captured in inshore waters of England and Wales. The juveniles of Raja microocellata were most common in shallow water, and the limited data available for R. undulata also indicates that any nursery grounds for this species would also be in shallow water. Juveniles of the genus Leucoraja occurred further offshore, although only the eggcases of L. naevus were recorded regularly on trawl surveys (with an L. fullonica eggcase recorded just once). The earliest free-living stages also occurred offshore. An improved knowledge of spawning and nursery grounds can be used to aid fisheries management and marine spatial planning, and may also inform the emerging interest in Important Shark and Ray Areas (ISRAs).

3549: All elasmobranchs are fully protected from fishing practices in Israel. In this ‘safe haven’, research led by the Morris Kahn Marine Research Station’s Marine Apex Predator Laboratory has shown that dusky sharks (Carcharhinus obscurus) and sandbar sharks (C. plumbeus) return to aggregate in the winter months (November-May) along the Israeli coastline (1-20 m depth; est. 80-100 individuals). We expect that they inhabit these areas due to the warm water discharge relative to the ambient winter temperatures (22-25°C from the power plant; ambient 16-18°C). Ours is the only long-term catch-and-release programme in the Mediterranean Basin. Currently, both species belong to Annex III of the Barcelona Convention and are evaluated as ‘Data Deficient and ‘Endangered’ on the IUCN Mediterranean Red List, respectively. Female sandbar sharks are increasingly observed with each tagging season in Israel and since 2018, we have proof that the dusky sharks are inhabiting this space during some stage of their gestation, yet we still do not know where their parturition grounds are. To answer this, we collaborated with Dr James Sulikowski, leading expert of shark reproductive biology, and co-developer of the innovative Birth-Alert Tag with Lotek Wireless. With funding from National Geographic, this state-of-the-art intrauterine satellite tag was deployed in one gravid dusky shark in April 2023 after confirmation of pregnancy via ultrasonogram, with further samples taken for physiological analyses. Further detections of this shark via acoustic transmitter were made until late May, which is unusual for this species. We present this suite of information relating to non-invasive methods.
Session 1: Insights into the spatial ecology of elasmobranch fish
3550: Horizontal and vertical movements of marine organisms are reflective of habitat preference and behavioural patterns in activity. Since the development of electronic monitoring devices, studies into the migrations and movements of many marine species are increasing. However, such studies into the vertical movements of benthic predators remain understudied. In this study, blonde skates, Raja brachyura, and spotted skates, R. montagui, were tagged with ‘pop-off’ data storage tags in the North Sea and English Channel. Diel vertical migrations, time-at-depth profiles and activity budgets were used to determine space-use patterns and preferences concerned with depth and temperature for mature individuals. The outcomes of this research will contribute a deeper understanding of the underlying processes that drive fish movements and distribution
Session 1: Insights into the spatial ecology of elasmobranch fish
3551: Distribution of species across regulatory and physical boundaries poses a recognised challenge to effective management and research, and these transboundary species tend to suffer more-severe population declines. Large pelagic sharks like the porbeagle, Lamna nasus, are particularly vulnerable due to their life history characteristics including their highly migratory behaviour, whereby the latter is particularly challenging for management in European waters where management jurisdictions change over small spatial scales. We used high-resolution satellite tags to demonstrate that individual porbeagles in the region display high inter-individual variation in behaviour, undertaking very rapid movements (up to 100 km per day) through multiple EEZs and physical habitats, transiting different management zones in a matter of days along different paths. These data highlight the value of existing and the urgent need for continued regional collaboration and cross-border funding mechanisms to maximise research impact to fill knowledge gaps and improve conservation outcomes for vulnerable and highly mobile shark species.
Session 1: Insights into the spatial ecology of elasmobranch fish
3552: Identifying the timing of key life history events, such as mating, is important for conserving endangered species. Yet, for many elasmobranchs, there is a paucity of data on reproductive timings. Developing low-cost and non-invasive methods for estimating elasmobranch reproductive timings could assist in closing the knowledge gap and aid collecting reproductive information on more species. The flapper skate (Dipturus intermedius) is a critically endangered elasmobranch and the largest skate found in European waters. A large flapper skate photo-ID database exists, featuring photographs taken throughout the year provided by members of the public. Here, we present novel work making opportunistic use of the flapper skate photo-ID database to estimate flapper skate reproductive timing. A methodology was developed to identify the occurrence of three indicators of reproductive activity visible in photographs: pelvic swelling, bite wounds, and scratch wounds. Over 2000 images were examined for presence of each indicator and the seasonality of their occurrence was analysed via generalised additive models. Results suggest flapper skate mate over winter and lay eggs in winter and spring. The findings are corroborated by existing literature, supporting the approach as a valid method for estimating elasmobranch reproductive timing. The developed approach for analysing images could be applied to other species and make use of citizen science, providing another route for understanding reproduction in elusive elasmobranchs.
Session 2: Citizen science I: The utility of social media and Local Ecological Knowledge
3553: A huge gap in environmental information exists in conflict regions where access to scientists ranges from unsafe to impossible. Previously unknown knowledge of Elasmobranchii presence, composition, and distribution can provide valuable fisheries information regarding the exploitation of elasmobranch species and for creating comprehensive conservation strategies. However, the diversity, ecology, behavior, and many other characteristics of these species in conflict zones remain virtually unknown, which is a major cause for concern. Traditional species assessments rely on in-situ observations, market surveys, and regulatory authorities forcing fisheries to self-report their catch. Conflict areas present a unique challenge, lacking formal regulation or scientific access. Here, we report the first use of social media monitoring for the extent of the Elasmobranch fishery in the Gaza Strip (east Mediterranean), a conflict region previously lacking any information. Our database consists of 3 years of daily reported catch from 16 fish stores and social media fishery-related influencers in the Gaza Strip. We collected 1530 data points belonging to 4619 individuals of 20 species. The analysis of the data sheds light on previously unknown temporal, spatial, and seasonal trends in elasmobranch catch distribution and relations to changes in the access to maritime areas due to local conflict escalations. We demonstrate this approach as a relatively accurate and inexpensive data mining procedure, allowing the quantification and normalization of multiple observations of caught and targeted fish into a uniformed geo-spatial-temporal system- making it a prime candidate for future endeavors in other data-poor regions and conflict zones in coastal areas.

3554: The environment sector, including organisations working to protect the marine environment, is the second-least diverse in the UK. There is an urgent need to address barriers to participation and diversify opportunities for involvement in conservation and research, as the marine environment has a vital role in natural, cultural, social and economic heritage for all communities. Project SIARC (Sharks Inspiring Action and Research with Communities) uses flagship elasmobranchs in Wales (angelshark, blue skate, common stingray, flapper skate, spurdog, and tope) to bring together local communities, fishers, researchers and government to cultivate a new appreciation and open-up access to the underwater environment in Wales. A major part of our work is to identify approaches that enable a wider range of people to engage with marine conservation in Wales and tackle the lack of diversity and inclusion within Project SIARC, thereby contributing to wider systemic change. We are on the start of our journey and to-date have focused on Project SIARC’s community initiatives in North Wales. Meetings, interviews and discussions with local communities allowed us to listen and learn from personal experiences, gathering information to produce a draft ‘Equity, Diversity and Inclusion Strategy’. This presentation will share the approach we have taken to date and some of the key learnings Project SIARC is a collaboration led by the Zoological Society of London and Natural Resources Wales, with six partners and several collaborators. It is made possible thanks to Welsh Government’s Nature Networks Fund, National Lottery Heritage Fund and On the EDGE Conservation.

3555: Large urban and industrial settlements, and the intense maritime traffic make the Mediterranean one of the most polluted areas in the world. This basin hosts considerable marine biodiversity, including many elasmobranchs, which are extremely vulnerable to environmental contamination due their life history traits. The impact of this threat on the cartilaginous fishes is still poorly studied, as well as the possible consequences for human health, in case of consumption of sharks, are uncertain. To fill this knowledge gap, quantitative and qualitative assessments of three groups of persistent organic pollutants (POPs) were carried out in the muscle and liver of two shark species, Mustelus punctulatus and Mustelus mustelus, caught in the Marine Protected Area (MPA) of Egadi Islands (South-Central Mediterranean Sea) between 2021 and 2023. As sharks are one of the top predators inhabiting the MPA, they can be considered a bioindicator of the local environmental status. Paradoxically, although M. punctulatus and M. mustelus have considerable commercial value for human consumption in the MPA, they are listed as Vulnerable by the IUCN in the Mediterranean. Regarding POPs levels, the results showed a trend of PCBs > DDTs >> HCB in liver and muscle for both species. Our results can significantly contribute to clarify the toxicological status of these species, allowing a first evaluation of the real risks both for the local marine life and for human health.

3556: Very little is known about the biology and ecology of the nursehound shark Scyliorhinus stellaris (Linnaeus, 1758), a medium-sized catshark in severe decline in the Mediterranean Sea, assessed as Near Threatened (Vulnerable in the Atlantic) by the IUCN. Here we present results emerging from the first 10 years of the Stellaris project (2013-2023), an underwater field monitoring project in the largest egg-case nursery area known in Italian waters, the Santa Croce Bank (Gulf of Naples, Central Tyrrhenian Sea). This ongoing citizen science project provides insights on basic reproductive information on this species in the wild, such as: seasonality, development, predation and natural mortality rates, and indications that this nursery area is in decline. Photo-identification reveals that this area is also a resting area for adults of both sexes, which is used year-round and over multiple years. This nursery area is a no-fishing zone and falls within a Natura 2000 site. In spite of its protected status, illegal fishing occurs as the whole Gulf is subject to intense artisanal and recreational fishing pressure. Results of the Stellaris project allowed the Santa Croce Bank to be identified by the IUCN as an ISRA, an Important Shark and Ray Area, highlighting the importance of this refuge and the need for increased management and conservation actions for this neglected species. These results also highlight the value of citizen science in making tangible conservation contribution.

3557: Sharks and rays in the Red Sea region are under intense fishing pressure, heavy development, and extensive tourism load. The IUCN report on the status of sharks and rays in the Arabian Sea and adjacent waters from 2017 found that at least half of the species are endangered. Based on these species assessments, in the Red Sea alone the number of endangered species is alarmingly higher, presenting a state of danger to almost all cartilaginous fish species that live in it. Research, conservation, and enforcement are scarce in the region. We have established a citizen science project SRS (sharks and rays in the Red Sea), based on the MECO Protocol, collecting observations from the public through social networks with the aim of gathering up-to-date basic biological and ecological information. Over 2,500 observations have been collected to date, mostly from the Gulf of Aqaba. Observations include 18 species of batoids and 14 species of sharks (82% and 18%, respectively). Our collected data has added new species records to the Gulf of Aqaba region and revealed information about their seasonality, reproduction, and distribution. These data provide essential ecological information in a region that is largely understudied and is crucial for planning conservation and management in the future.

3558: Angelsharks, Squatina squatina, can be seen relatively frequently by divers and fishers in the Canary Islands, a unique stronghold for the species. Due to their benthic ecology and coastal location, angelsharks are particularly susceptible to accidental capture in fisheries and habitat degradation. As a result of this, angelsharks are now listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species. In 2019, angelsharks were listed under the Spanish Endangered Species List for Canary Island waters as "In danger of extinction", the highest level of protection within this legislation. Following this listing, the development of a Recovery Plan was mandated, which sets out suitable measures for the management and conservation of angelsharks. Angel Shark Project: Canary Islands (ASP:CI) conducted a comprehensive series of in-person and online surveys to compile crucial information regarding angelshark interactions, perceptions, and potential protective measures, involving three primary interaction groups: divers, recreational fishers, and commercial fishers. This information, combined with ASP:CI scientific research, was augmented by a collaborative workshop, which engaged stakeholders representing various interests. Together, these efforts facilitated the identification of conservation areas and the co-designing of specific measures to ensure the future preservation of Angelsharks within their expansive stronghold. This presentation will delineate the key findings derived from this work, emphasizing the importance of employing a participatory approach in designing conservation strategies for this Critically Endangered species. This work, led by ASP:CI, was funded by Shark Conservation Fund and through a contract with the Canary Islands Government, co-financed by the FEDER 2014-2020 Operational Program.

3559: Spurdog (Squalus acanthias), otherwise known as Spiny or Picked Dogfish, are members of the dogfish (Squalidae) family. They are distinguished by the presence of a spine in front of each dorsal fin. They have a wide distribution, mainly inhabiting temperate waters. This species was originally listed on the IUCN Red List as Critically Endangered, but through a non-genuine change in 2015, Spurdog was changed to Endangered in Europe (IUCN, 2015). In the Northeast Atlantic, there has been a fishery for Spurdog since the early 20th century. This population was overexploited which led to population decline. Various management measures have been put in place to aid recovery of this population, including placing Spurdog on the Prohibited species list. In 2022, ICES gave advice that the population could support a fishery for 2023 and 2024. In 2023, the fishery was reopened with a TAC of 17,353 tonnes (t) across the region. The UK has a quota of 4,825 t in Western waters and 2,781 t in the North Sea. As of October 2023, 194.0 t (4.0%) and 95.0 t (4.6%) of these quotas have been landed respectively. This presentation discusses the management history of Spurdog and the possible dangers of reopening a fishery on tentative signs of recovery.
3560: The spurdog (Squalus acanthias Linnaeus, 1758) Northeast Atlantic stock is managed as a single unit and has undergone a long period of overfishing, especially in the 1950s/1960s, which has caused its population to collapse. There are now signs of population growth but it remains listed as “Endangered” and overexploitation may have had an impact on its genetic composition. Limited data are available on the stocks genetic structure and properly delineating a stock unit for fisheries management is crucial to allow sustainability of the exploited population. Population genetics provides valuable insights into connectivity and genetic distinctions among individuals from different areas. Looking at genetic diversity within and between populations is also important in terms of population resilience in the face of climate change or other pressures such as overexploitation. A first assessment of the population structure was done using the NADH dehydrogenase subunit 2 (ND2) mitochondrial marker sequenced from 48 spurdogs sampled along the Norwegian part of the Northeast Atlantic. 25 unique haplotypes were distinguished, showing high genetic diversity in Norwegian waters, but no genetic distinction between sampling locations. To provide more accurate population level data, over 89 individuals from identical locations were used for genome-wide analysis, involving 53492 single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) derived from Restriction-site associated DNA sequencing (RAD-seq). Clustering analysis revealed subpopulations along Norwegian waters. This study presents this population structure and discusses their relevance for regional fishery management purposes.
3561: In the ocean, mobile species exhibit diverse movements across different spatial and temporal scales. Understanding the drivers behind these movements is essential for effective management and predicting responses to a changing ocean environment. A multitude of environmental cues, such as temperature and salinity, have been shown to affect the movements of elasmobranch species. However, it is increasingly recognized that social drivers may also influence movement. We conducted an acoustic telemetry study in a partially enclosed sea loch on the west coast of Scotland to investigate the movements and habitat selection of spurdog (Squalus acanthias). Spurdog segregate based on size and sex, and these subgroups display a high range of movements, from transatlantic movements to coastal residency. Some subgroups also display high levels of relatedness, suggesting kinship bonds within subgroups. Our findings revealed that spurdog exhibited a high level of year-round residency within the loch and that temperature plays a pivotal role in their habitat selection. Additionally, subgroups within the population display different habitat choices, which may be caused by underlying population social processes. This study underscores the importance of understanding all drivers of animal movement. Identifying sites that promote residential behaviour can aid in developing effective management strategies for species, like the spurdog. However, it is equally crucial to comprehend the social drivers of movement, as they can significantly influence habitat choices. By considering the interplay between environmental and social factors, we can gain a more comprehensive understanding of animal movements and enhance conservation efforts for these mobile ocean species.
3562: Spiny dogfish (Squalus acanthias) is an Endangered top predator with an antitropical distribution, including extensive use of the fjords in southern and western Norway. Increasingly, these fjords are subjected to warming surface water temperatures and hypoxic bottom water. Habitat compression of spiny dogfish is predicted to instigate increased conflict between the sharks and the fisheries and aquaculture industries. To investigate if varying oxygen levels affect their depth use, we tagged more than 80 spiny dogfish with acoustic transmitters instrumented with depth, acceleration, and temperature sensors to reveal any spatiotemporal depth patterns. Furthermore, spiny dogfish swim in groups based on sex and/or size, thus a social network analysis was performed to check whether the tagged individuals exhibited interactions across time or space. Preliminary results indicate that the spiny dogfish utilize an extensive part of the water column, and most tagged individuals interact with several other spiny dogfish.

3563: In the Northern Adriatic Sea (FAO-GSA 17), fishery exploitation of marine resources influenced communities and the ecosystem (Sguotti et al., 2022). In the last decades, elasmobranch species, characterized by slow growth rate and low fecundity, have been depleted due to fishing activities (Barausse et al., 2014; Ferretti et al., 2013). Despite being landed as by-catch or seasonal target catch, first evidence of population increase in abundance is highlighted for the smooth hounds (Mustelus spp.), while the spiny dogfish (Squalus acanthias) continues to decline (Maioli et al., 2023). Since several approaches suggested the occurrence of seasonal movements of these species (Manfredi et al., 2010; Bonanomi et al., 2018; Barbato et al., 2021), this study aims at identifying: (i) seasonal use of space of these species using fishery-dependent data from bottom otter trawls (OTB) collected within the European Data Collection Framework; (ii) spatial hotspots of observed landing per unit effort (LPUE) from coupled VMS and logbook OTB data; (iii) preliminary movement ecology aspects using conventional tagging (2017-2023) and acoustic telemetry (2022-2023) at individual-level. The first objectives allowed to identify a different seasonal use of space between the smooth hounds and the spiny dogfish, seasonal hotspot of LPUE and refined identification of areas where young-of-the-year, juveniles and adults occur. In addition, preliminary results of movement ecology highlighted site fidelity, residency and transboundary movement at individual level. Given the lack of management measures for such species, the combination of these approaches can provide essential information to set effective spatial management measures for these species.
