3564: Mobile sharks are more at risk of encountering human activities such as fisheries, putting high bycatch pressure on shark populations. Spurdog (Squalus acanthias) was historically exploited by a well-documented fishery, however, relatively little is known about their large-scale movements, habitat preferences, and population dynamics after the stock collapse in the late 1990s. Over the past years, we used a variety of data types and methods, like trawl and longline surveys, fishery bycatch and environmental data, dissections, satellite tagging and spatial mapping, to decipher the spatial distribution, movement patterns, diet and life history composition of spurdog in Norwegian and northern Northeast Atlantic (NEA) waters. We found that they prefer relatively warm and shallow waters (<150 m) and stay close within coastal waters while exhibiting diel vertical migrations. The latter could imply them following their prey, which we identified as mainly bony fishes based on >500 analysed stomachs. Based on overall 5,000 dissected individuals mainly from fisheries bycatch, we found that the recruitment may have increased considerably faster in the recent two decades than previously projected, which resulted in a gradually younger population of gravid females (50% maturity at 9.3 years). This faster population recovery is reflected in the new assessment of the NEA spurdog stock by the International Council for the Exploration of the Sea. The resulting fishing quota for the first time since 2009, makes close monitoring and efforts to increase our understanding of its dynamics, population structure, and responses to changing environmental conditions even more important.
3565: The success of international conservation agreements relies on proper implementation at the national level. Because elasmobranchs are considered both commodities and wildlife, governments’ approaches to associated fisheries and environment treaty obligations are often misaligned. Scrutiny of this performance is lacking and represents a core yet surmountable challenge to effective policies and ultimate population rebuilding. The Shark League (a coalition including Shark Trust, Ecology Action Centre, and Shark Advocates International) will soon release a gap analysis that examines the effects of Atlantic shark and ray protection measures under various treaties, primarily the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES) and the International Commission for Conservation of Atlantic Tunas (ICCAT). Based on an evaluation of the performance of ICCAT Parties and Cooperators with respect to various obligations for CITES-listed elasmobranchs, we highlight key gaps between concrete restrictions and conservation needs. Recommendations for priority improvements at national and international levels extend beyond government action to include specific suggestions for elasmobranch conservationists and interested scientists. Aims focus on better integration of fisheries and environmental agency activities to fulfill elasmobranch policy commitments across treaties, but also include improved fisheries and trade information, more rigorous conservation standards, and expanded assistance, as well as new safeguards for under-protected species. Because overfishing is the primary driver of shark and ray depletion, bridging these divides is critical to securing a brighter outlook for elasmobranchs in the Atlantic and beyond.

3566: The evaluation of policy effectiveness and impact is a crucial step in the policy cycle, to see if the agreed targets are met and to give guidance for improving future policies and legislation. One of the fundamental European Union (EU) Directives for Nature Conservation, the Habitats Directive, did not include conservation of elasmobranchs at the time it was drafted in 1992 and has not been updated to address this gap in the 30 years since. This means that elasmobranchs do not feature in Nature2000, which forms the basis for protected areas. However, the Marine Strategy Framework Directive (MSFD) from 2008, opened a window of opportunity for elasmobranch- related measures both in spatial protection and fisheries management, but has it delivered? Here, we assessed EU Member States’ (EU MS) efforts to integrate elasmobranchs in their national monitoring and programmes of measures under the MSFD, and if these filled in the gaps between EU policies. Results are mixed: whilst some EU MS, such as the Netherlands and Italy, report shark-specific measures under the MSFD, others generally refer to existing obligations in relation to monitoring and conservation under EU, international, and regional legal frameworks. There are no Marine Protected Areas set up under the MSFD that aim to protect elasmobranchs specifically in any EU MS. Based on the review of EU MS reporting under the MSFD, we provide advice on furthering shark conservation at EU level and how this relates to contemporary legal and policy developments in the EU and at international level.

A synthesis of 10 years of follow up was produced giving elements on the estimation of amount of money the diversity of species and geographic origins of the different pieces. The results the juridical victories are discussed in the context of global urgency for marine biodiversity worldwide.

3568: The Netherlands Shark and Ray Action Plan (SARAP) dates from 2017. It was reviewed in 2021 and there is currently a new action plan which will run until 2027. The objectives of the SARAP fall under Descriptor 1 of the Marine Strategy Framework Directive (MSFD) ‘Biodiversity’ and aim to improve the population size, distribution and condition of sharks and rays in Dutch waters. Nine of the 15 actions in the plan address European Regulations, Frameworks and Directives, as well as international conventions. All require international cooperation. These actions are not new and have been on the European agenda for a number of years. Since 2017 the EU STECF (Scientific, Technical, Economic Commission for Fisheries) has initiated three expert working groups specifically on elasmobranchs, covering skate and ray management, the implementation of the EU regulation on finning and assessment of the impact of the 2009 European Community Shark Action Plan. These meetings resulted in recommendations to advance the management and conservation of the species. Concurrently, the ICES Working Group Elasmobranch Fishes provides the science to improve stock assessments and to advise on fishing opportunities. In the past years new species have been listed on CITES (Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Flora and Fauna) and CMS (Convention on Migratory Species), leading to obligations from the contracting parties. Although some progress is being made, real change has yet to take place. This paper will present the Netherlands Shark and Ray Action Plan as a case study in international cooperation.
3569: Effective conservation measures are urgently needed for elasmobranchs. People possess significant power in driving conservation efforts, but elasmobranchs, known for historically evoking irrational attitudes, have been overlooked. Educational events improving peoples’ perception might aid conservation action. Fishery management measures are also necessary, but fishers’ willingness to adopt them must be assessed. To investigate propensity for conservation, the LIFE ELIFE project (Elasmobranchs Low-Impact Fishing Experience LIFE18 NAT/IT/000846) aims at evaluating stakeholders’ attitude and the impact of educational events using questionnaires/interviews. Participating to educational events improved people’s attitude towards elasmobranchs. Respondents indicating fear and danger as the main feelings decreased from 22.0% and 29.8% in the group not experiencing educational events (N=542) to 11.2% and 14.6% in the group that experienced them (N=121). Moreover, the percentage of respondents thinking that elasmobranchs are endangered (76.8% versus 84.8%), that more species should be protected (77.3% versus 88.9%), and of those willing to change their behaviours to aid elasmobranchs’ conservation (92.9% versus 100%) increased. Regarding fishers (N=136), only 16.0% reported a perception of decrease in elasmobranch abundances; however, fishers stated that their category should contribute to elasmobranchs’ conservation (70.4%) and that some species should be protected (50.7%). Despite 56.3% of fishers were not aware of potential fishery management measures (i.e., gear modifications), when informed, 60.9% declared they would adopt them. These preliminary results are promising; people’s positive attitude can be used to urge decision makers to adopt concrete conservation initiatives, which are likely to be more easily accepted by fishers given their willingness to collaborate.

3570: We present the results of a Gap analysis carried out in the summer of 2023 on the elasmobranchs of the Southeastern Caribbean. The geographical scope of this project concerns the whole of the Lesser Antilles, as well as the Dominican Republic, Haiti and Jamaica to the west, and the exclusive economic zones of the countries and territories of the Guiana plateau to the southeast. As most of this area encompasses the waters of Small Island Developing States (SIDS) and other small autonomous nations the marine life in general has not been extensively studied. Our approach was threefold, firstly we focussed on establishing an overview of the species present in the area and the research effort that had gone in to them, secondly we made an overview of the research conducted in the waters of all countries in our area of interest and lastly we made an overview of existing conservation and management measures and the level to which these were implemented. We based our findings on information gathered through a literature review as well as from interviews with regional and local experts. The research is part of the CAMAC project, for CAribbean marine Megafauna and anthropogenic Activities led by the SPAW Regional Activities Centre. The CAMAC project works to improve knowledge Caribbean mega fauna (mammals, sharks & rays and turtles) and strengthen regional collaboration. The aim is to provide recommendations and tools to reduce the negative impacts of interactions between marine megafauna and human activities.
3571: The presence of spiny butterfly rays, Gymnura altavela, in waters less than 20 m deep off the Canary Islands shows marked seasonality, with relatively high abundances in the summer and autumn. Large aggregations of sometimes hundreds of individuals, primarily females, appear in specific shallow areas of the archipelago and seem to be associated with the seasonal variation in water temperature. This seasonal pattern of presence or absence in shallow areas suggests that spiny butterfly rays migrate into deeper waters or other unknown areas during the rest of the year. G. altavela shows sexual dimorphism; in our study, females were larger and more abundant than males, with a sex ratio of 1:18.9. The species’ estimated asymptotic length, L∞, was 183.75 cm and thus close to the common length reported for the species (200 cm). The von Bertalanffy growth constant (k) oscillated between 0.210 and 0.310 year−1, as similarly described for the species in the Western North Atlantic off the U.S. coast. From June to November, the seawater temperature oscillated between 19 and 24 ◦C, and massive aggregations of females occurred at 22–24 ◦C and in a few specific sandy beaches on the islands. Spiny butterfly rays, mostly females, show a preference for aggregating in shallow waters during summertime, probably conditionate to mating or breeding behaviour.

3572: The Cabo de Palos-Islas Hormigas marine reserve in Southeast Spain stands as an outstanding conservation model, boasting one of the highest fish biomasses among Mediterranean Marine Protected Areas (MPAs). However, just beyond its boundaries, populations of highly threatened elasmobranchs appear to critically rely on this area unnoticed and unprotected. Since March 2023, over a hundred photographs from divers, snorkelers, and fishers have been collected and analysed, revealing the area´s potential significance for the Common Guitarfish (Rhinobatos rhinobatos), the Spiny Butterfly Ray (Gymnura altavela), the Common Stingray (Dasyatis pastinaca) and the Common Eagle Ray (Myliobatis aquila). Remarkably, these records indicate the annual presence of the once-though-extinct in the Western Mediterranean Common Guitarfish, with potentially pregnant females appearing in June and newborns in September. Additionally, further evidence is needed to confirm the occurrence of the Giant Guitarfish (Glaucostegus cemiculus) according to some reported pictures due to identification issues. These photographs suggest fisheries-induced mortality due to illegal retention and inadequate handling techniques is occurring to an unknown extent. Also, pregnant individuals and newborns of Spiny Butterfly Ray can be seen yearly throughout the summer, as well as potential aggregations of likely young-of-the-year of Common Stingray. Opportunistic scientific expeditions have further allowed us to document annual aggregations of 15-40 individuals of Common Eagle Ray with unknown function. These preliminary findings highlight the Murcia Eastern Coast as a potential conservation realm for highly endangered elasmobranch species. However, further research efforts are needed and warranted to inform effective management actions to ensure their survival.

3573: Establishing how threatened wildlife are distributed spatially and temporally is essential for effective conservation and management planning. While many shark species are threatened globally, knowledge on sex-specific differences in behaviour and fine-scale habitat use remains limited, hindering the implementation of appropriate conservation actions. Here, acoustic telemetry was used to investigate sex-specific space use in the Critically Endangered angelshark Squatina squatina in the Canary Islands (Atlantic Ocean), a key stronghold for the species. We collected data on space use, residency and movement of adult males (n = 32) and females (n = 72) in Spain’s largest marine reserve (La Graciosa Marine Reserve) over 4 yr (2018−2022). Presence in offshore sites (>80 m depth) indicated long-term utilisation of deep-water habitat, not previously observed in this species. Males were more likely to be detected in deep water and displayed significantly greater levels of activity and roaming behaviour than females. Patterns of behaviour in shallow waters indicated both social and habitat sexual segregation. Diel variability was also recorded, with greater activity occurring nocturnally. This study demonstrates the importance of considering the spatiotemporal distribution of both sexes, horizontally and vertically, when designing effective conservation measures.

3574: In 2023, three records of angelshark stress-induced births onboard fishing vessels in Türkiye were recorded. The first record was from Fethiye Bay in January 2023, in which three Squatina oculata pups were aborted on the vessel, with one external yolk sac still attached, with the pups deceased pups. The second account was of five Squatina squatina pups aborted onboard a fishing vessel from the Dardanelles, in which all pups survived, and the last account was also from Fethiye Bay in March, 2023, this time in which three pups survived. This last account provides the only recent account on Squatina oculata reproduction from the last two decades. The pups were approximately 19.5 cm, 21.5 cm and 23 cm total length, with an internal yolk sac which could be seen iridescently through the body, estimated at about 3-4 cm in width. These records also provide important details of reproductive habitats, spawning grounds and spawning seasons, which seems to ocur in spring in Turkey. The data presents a new much smaller minimum maturity size for S. oculata. Also, data were summarized from citizen science records for Turkish sharks and rays along with other records directly from fishers providing a total of 51 previously unpublished angel shark records for Turkey, and highlighting three potential Critical Angel Shark Areas (CASAs) in Turkey; Fethiye Bay, Çanakkale Strait and Antalya Bay. We stress the need for better protection of these areas, along with scientific monitoring of these sites to learn more about these species.

3575: The smoothnose wedgefish (Rhynchobatus laevis) is a critically endangered shark-like ray that has received limited research attention. To address knowledge gaps in its behaviour and movement patterns, this study utilized satellite tagging over a 51-day period in the Arabian Gulf. Based on the resulting movement track, the specimen covered a minimum distance of 712 km, traversing the exclusive economic zones of three different countries. Its track began in the United Arab Emirates, from where it headed north, entering Iranian waters where it spent the majority of its time, before continuing westward across the Arabian Gulf and eventually reaching Qatari waters. Novel insights in its behaviour recorded a pattern of rapid ascent over the study period. Even though these ascents these ascents were observed both diurnal and nocturnal, they occurred predominately in the latter. Contrary to the prevailing belief that wedgefish are bottom-associated, the study animal spent a considerable amount of its time in the water column. Its use of a variety of depths in both nearshore and offshore waters highlights a potential susceptibility to multiple fishing year types. This underscores the need for an international, cooperative approach to the management and conservation of shark-like rays in the Arabian Gulf.

3576: The Canary Islands, located in the Atlantic Ocean off the northwest coast of Africa, have quickly become an idyllic place for elasmobranch species that inhabit their waters, primarily due to the absence of industrial fishing and the use of harmful fishing methods such as trawling. In the Canary Islands, fishing activities consist mainly of small-scale artisanal fishing and recreational fishing, which is gaining popularity and attracting more enthusiasts each year. However, sharks and rays are generally not targeted species in these fishing activities. Only dogfish sharks and various species within this family are intentionally fished or captured as bycatch in the islands. This is primarily due to the use of their meat for human consumption as "tollos", a typical food of the archipelago made with the dehydrated meat of these sharks. Currently, our knowledge of these species is limited to data derived from artisanal fishermen and their captures, which, as often is the case in many parts of the world, are underestimated due to poor or non-existent proper identification of each species. Including biological data (species, sexes) and/or ecological data (preferred areas, depths, or seasons), severely limiting their proper assessment or manage. In this study, the current status of these species in the Canary Islands is evaluated, aiming to identify the situation of each species as accurately as possible.

3577: The Angel Shark Project was established with the aim of securing the future of Critically Endangered angel sharks (Squatina squatina, S. aculeata and S. oculata) across the range. Among other regions, the Canary Islands, Wales, Libya, Greece, Corsica, Croatia and Ireland were identified as important and unique areas for at least one of the three angel shark species. The data gathered in these regions has contributed to the implementation of targeted conservation measures across the Eastern Atlantic and Mediterranean Sea and to deliver priority policy outcomes across six countries. This two-way exchange of information between partners across the angel shark species’ ranges has been vital to better coordinate conservation action. This presentation will highlight some of the key milestones from the different regions, including enhancing legal protection in priority countries, co-developing regional action plans to minimise threats and promoting the sustainability of shark and ray fishing.

3578: The Angel Shark Conservation Network (ASCN) was established by the authors in 2016, to empower action to restore and safeguard angel shark populations throughout their natural range. To date, focusing on the Eastern Atlantic and Mediterranean Sea, which encompasses the range of three Critically Endangered angel shark species: Squatina aculeata, S. oculata, and S. squatina. The ASCN aims to facilitate dialogue and information sharing on angel shark conservation efforts and provides a mechanism for developing strategic conservation planning documents at different geographic scales. A number of Action Plans have been developed via multidisciplinary workshops, sitting underneath the Eastern Atlantic and Mediterranean Angel Shark Conservation Strategy. These documents aim to identify the key actions needed to overcome major threats to angel sharks in each specific region to guide future research, management, policy, and conservation. Progress towards actions outlined in these documents will be discussed, highlighting how far we have come and what we have left to achieve. The ASCN actively encourages individuals and organisations to deliver actions outlined in the angel shark conservation planning documents, facilitating a collaborative approach, and working in partnership to support and deliver angel shark conservation. Various levels of ASCN membership exist, and recent work has been undertaken to better formalise this process. This presentation will outline the ASCN’s re-launch, with clearer guidance on how to get involved and hopes to expand the network to enable further action for angel sharks across their range. This work is funded by Shark Conservation Fund.

3579: Human-wildlife interactions are crucial in shaping our understanding of nature and can significantly impact efforts to conserve endangered species and their habitats. As human activities continue to expand in the marine environment, encounters between humans and marine wildlife are expected to rise. Addressing and incorporating these interactions into conservation plans can provide valuable insights and bolster conservation efforts. In this study, we utilized the Marxan software to analyze data from the MECO citizen science project, focusing on two guitarfish species, the blackchin guitarfish (Glaucostegus cemiculus) and the common guitarfish (Rhinobatos rhinobatos), along the Mediterranean coast of Israel. Our objective was to identify areas of high probability for human encounters with guitarfish species while considering the specific activities conducted during these interactions. Our findings revealed that human activities varied across different areas during guitarfish encounters. By incorporating human activities as conservation targets in the Marxan analysis, in addition to guitarfish distribution data, we observed no significant shifts in the location of areas marked for conservation. However, the total area of these conservation zones increased significantly. This approach demonstrates how incorporating data on human-wildlife interactions can enhance conservation modeling efforts. Moreover, our study highlights the significance of including a social dimension in conservation planning, offering a fresh perspective on the process. By integrating human-wildlife interaction data, conservation strategies can be better tailored to specific locations and activities, facilitating more effective protection for guitarfish species and their habitats.

3580: In June 2022, an initial expedition comprising members from the Fundación Oceanogràfic, Seville Aquarium, and LAMNA Association certified the presence of juvenile and adult 'guitarrón' or blackchin guitarfish (Glaucostegus cemiculus) within the protected waters of Doñana National Park in Huelva, Spain. 3581: Environmental DNA (eDNA) methodologies allow us to assess biodiversity by taking samples from the environment (e.g water, sediment or air) and extracting DNA from the samples to identify the presence of species. We designed an eDNA survey to gather information on elasmobranch presence in the Carmarthen Bay and Estuaries (CBAE) Special Area of Conservation (SAC) in South Wales. Sampling sites were informed using hydrodynamic and tracer modelling based on residual patterns, led by Bangor University. Water samples were taken from 10 sites across CBAE SAC each month, for 12 months. These data were brought together with samples taken in 2020/2021 by Angel Shark Project: Wales, which covered 10 sites across 12 months in the Pen Llyn A’r Sarnau (PLAS) SAC in North Wales. Further samples were taken and analysed concurrently with BRUVS surveys in the PLAS SAC. A total of eleven elasmobranch species were detected across the two SACs, including all four Project SIARC focal species – angelshark, common stingray, spurdog and tope. This presentation will highlight the key findings from these surveys. 3582: Skates (Rajiformes) represent one of the most intriguing cases of high species richness coupled with extremely conservative morphological and ecological traits. Small differences are described within and between species and increasing cases of cryptic speciation have been recorded among sister and non-sister taxa. More interestingly, this condition has been frequently observed in Central Atlantic Ocean (CAO), along the coasts of Western Africa, between Angola and Senegal, where oceanographic heterogeneities such as current systems, may play a key role for ecological speciation in skates. The use of multiple mtDNA loci and its integration with nuDNA microsatellite has been successfully applied to estimate the genetic variation in skate species inhabiting the CAO. Phylogenetic reconstructions, phylogeographic patterns and genetic connectivity estimates were applied to test the hypothesis that restricted gene flow and genetic divergence within Raja species reflect known climate and bio-oceanographic discontinuities. The widely distributed Raja miraletus species complex counts five deeply distinct lineages three of which co-occur in CAO: the Angolan Raja cf. miraletus, the Senegalese and sympatric R. parva and Raja cf. miraletus. In addition, an ancient, hidden lineage nesting in the clade Raja straeleni/R. clavata/R. maderensis was identified in Angola. The complexity of oceanographic system acting in the CAO (i.e., the Benguela Current region and the intertropical Canary current inflowing from the northeast) may have influenced the diversification of the Angolan and Senegalese taxa, boosting the biodiversity of the area, in an unprecedented anthology of species-specific evolutionary histories.

3583: Elasmobranchs, including the common stingray, are pivotal components of marine ecosystems, yet much remains to be understood about their habitat requirements and life history characteristics. The identification and investigation of nursery areas are critical for effective conservation and management, as these areas offer essential resources for the early life stages, contributing significantly to population sustainability. A nursery area of Common stingrays has been discovered in Liri Beach in 2018, on the eastern coast of central Greece. Adults and juveniles have been recorded at depths of 3 to 6 meters depth on a sandy soil bed. By employing field surveys, we have explored the presence and attributes of the common stingray's nursery area in the region. Our findings unveil a shallow, nearshore region that provides optimal environmental conditions for the growth and development of juvenile stingrays. These habitats afford protection against predation and facilitate access to abundant food resources, ensuring the successful survival and subsequent recruitment of young individuals into the adult population. Furthermore, we have examined the ecological interactions and connectivity between the identified nursery area in Central Greece and the surrounding habitats, underscoring the significance of considering broader ecological networks for effective conservation planning. By comprehending the spatial dynamics and connectivity patterns, we can devise strategies to safeguard and manage these critical areas, securing the long-term viability of the common stingray population.

3584: The Canary Islands was identified as a unique stronghold for the Angel shark (Squatina squatina), a species considered Critically Endangered according to the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species. Angelsharks inhabit coastal and shallow areas, being exposed to the effects of anthropogenic pollution, such as the accumulation of heavy metals. In this study, we analysed the concentration of twenty-one metals and trace elements in liver and muscle samples from dead specimens, nine from the Canary Islands and five from the Celtic Seas region (Wales and Ireland), using optical emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES), cold vapor atomic absorption spectroscopy (CV-AAS), and inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS). The results did not show sex as an influential factor in the concentration of heavy metals in the Canarian population. However, the size and weight of individuals were negatively correlated with Hg, Mo, B, and Cr in muscle, and positively correlated with Co, Fe, V, Mn, and Cr in the liver. These differences were more pronounced in a prenatal individual. The results indicate that growth may play a crucial role in the bioaccumulation and biomagnification of metals in organs. In terms of geographical distribution, we observed significant differences between the individuals from the Canary Islands and the Celtic Seas regarding the concentration of Hg, Cd, and Cr, which were higher in the Canary Islands, and Zn and Mn, which were higher in the Celtic Seas, likely due to differences in pollution levels between the two areas.

3585: According to the International Union for the Conservation of Nature (IUCN), around 50% of shark and ray species are facing high risk of extinction in the Mediterranean Sea. To date, the knowledge of elasmobranchs is fragmented and focused for certain species and areas of the basin with poor population assessment, especially in remote sites. The Pelagie Archipleago (Pelagie islands), is considered one of the most important hot-spot for sharks in the Mediterranean Sea. This area hosts a wide range of species potentially threatened by historical fishing pressure and habitat loss, especially large-bodied sharks, whose spatiotemporal patterns of abundance and distribution are poorly known. Evaluating historical dynamics of cartilaginous fish in the Pelagie archipelago can be very challenging and it can be crucial to understand their current population status. In the present study, we used LEK (Local Ecological Knowledge) through the historical memory and experience of fishers to collect information about the elasmobranch species inhabiting the Pelagie islands, with a particular focus of large-bodied sharks. Based on fishers’ perception, we recorded a dramatic reduction of large pelagic sharks over 60 years, mainly hammerheads (Sphyrna spp.) and sandbar sharks (Carcharhinus plumbeus). We also reconstructed the historical abundance of several elasmobranchs inhabiting the area. Our results provide important insights that can be used as a baseline for conservation initiatives in a shark data-poor region such as the Pelagie Archipelago.

3586: The western Mediterranean Sea is a region with a high diversity of chondrichthyan species; however, this region is subjected to a high discharge of pollutants, such as heavy metals. Consequently, owing to their ecological role, these species are prone to heavy metal bioaccumulation. Therefore, an assessment of the concentrations of three heavy metals present in the muscle tissue of 17 chondrichthyan species in the western Mediterranean Sea was performed. A total of 116 individuals were used, mainly caught by trawling and small-scale fishing. Lead (Pb), cadmium (Cd), and copper (Cu) were quantified using Microwave-Assisted Extraction (MAE) and Graphite Furnace Atomic Absorption Spectrometry (GF-AAS). Significant differences were observed between some species and taxonomic groups for Pb, Cd, and Cu. Among all the analysed species, the rabbit fish (Chimaera monstrosa) presented the highest concentration (mg/kg wet weight) of Pb (0.2924 ± 0.1689), of which some individuals exceeded the concentration threshold for Pb established by the Commission Regulation (EU) 2023/915. However, the velvet belly lanternshark (Etmopterus spinax) had the highest concentrations (mg/kg wet weight) of Cd (0.0622 ± 0.0244) and Cu (0.8179 ± 0.4167), exceeding the maximum concentration of Cd allowed by the (EU) 2023/915. A negative correlation between the concentration of Pb and trophic level was found, owing to the high concentrations found in low-trophic level species, such as C. monstrosa and E. spinax. Overall, the results obtained are important for human consumption. This is because these species are consumed and of great commercial interest in this region.

3587: The small-spotted catshark Scyliorhinus canicula, is a demersal Scyliorhinid shark species commonly found in Mediterranean and Northeastern Atlantic waters. The philopatric and sedentary nature of adult female individuals, along with its high abundance among bottom trawl bycatch; stock exploitation resilience and widespread distribution could support the xenobiotic biomonitoring potential of this species. Previous research on the subject concluded the specie´s muscle tissue is capable of reflecting space-time persistent Pb, Cd and Cu hotspots. To further explore such potential, interspecific monitoring has been attempted between Merluccius merluccius and S. canicula for which a total of 49 individuals of each species were gathered and data correlation was performed among individuals captured in the same haul. The Cd and Pb biomonitor potential of S. canicula egg capsules was also assessed. A total of 75 embryos were exposed via solution to different concentration ranges of these xenobiotics (Cd = 0.05-17.12 and Pb = 3-102.78 mg·Kg-1) for a 2.5 month period. All samples were analysed via GFAAS and matrices were digested via MAE techniques. High significant interspecific correlation values were observed in Cd and Pb concentrations between both species (Spearman r = 0.817 and 0.833 respectively) as well as moderate positive correlation for Cu (Spearman r = 0.633). Regarding Pb and Cd accumulation by egg capsules, high linearity was observed between dissolved concentrations of the elements and those found within the egg capsule (r2 = 0.98 and 0.96 respectively) with signifficant differences between trials occurring at higher Cd and Pb exposure concentrations.

3588: Microplastics (plastic particles sized under 5mm) are ubiquitous in the marine environment. They are known to have negative effects on marine organisms when ingested, including accumulation in digestive systems, causing starvation, and leaching of toxic chemicals, impacting development and reproduction. The habitat of reef manta rays (Mobula alfredi), a filter-feeding elasmobranch, overlaps with plastic pollution hotspots globally. This makes them at risk of ingesting the particles, with potential negative consequences on their fitness. The species is already listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red list, due to other anthropogenic pressures, such as fishing. It is therefore important to understand the risk of plastic pollution on this charismatic megafaunal species. This study is investigating the presence of microplastics in reef manta ray feeding grounds in the Chagos Archipelago. This is a no-take Marine Protected Area, home to a resident population of reef manta rays. However remote, the beaches of the Archipelago are covered in plastic debris which originates from elsewhere. This suggests there will be plenty of microplastics in the Archipelago waters. Quantifying the amount of microplastic in the water will build a better picture of how it could impact the local population of reef manta rays. It will also hopefully input into wider conversations about plastic reduction on remote islands.

3589: Environmental temperature affects physiological functions, representing a barrier for the range expansions of ectothermic species. To understand the link between thermal physiology and biogeography, a key question is whether among-species thermal sensitivity of metabolic rates is mechanistically constrained or buffered through physiological remodeling over evolutionary time. The former conception, the Universal Temperature Dependence hypothesis, predicts similar among- and within-species thermal sensitivity. The latter conception, the Metabolic Cold Adaptation hypothesis, predicts lower among-species thermal sensitivity than within-species sensitivity. Previous studies that tested these hypotheses for fishes overwhelmingly investigated teleosts with elasmobranchs understudied. Here, we show that among-species thermal sensitivity of resting metabolic rates is lower than within-species sensitivity in teleosts but not in elasmobranchs. Further, species richness declines with latitude more rapidly in elasmobranchs than in teleosts. Metabolic Cold Adaptation exhibited by teleosts might underpin their high diversity at high latitudes, whereas the inflexible thermal sensitivity approximated by Universal Temperature Dependence of elasmobranchs might explain their low diversity at high latitudes. These findings are discussed in the context of range expansions of sharks and rays, including recent examples from Ireland and the UK.

3590: One of the chief consequences of climate change is the worldwide redistribution of species in the pursue of physiologically and ecologically favourable conditions. As part of one of the most threatened groups of vertebrates, assessing how climate change may affect the distribution patterns of key shark species is essential for their long-term conservation and management. The present study aims to assess how climate change projections (based on the representative concentration pathways 2.6, 4.5, 6.0, and 8.5) for the middle and end of the century may affect the global patterns of habitat suitability (HS) for large hammerhead sharks – a unique and particularly threatened groups of elasmobranchs. Poleward shifts are projected for all three species, with considerable tropical declines for both S. lewini and S. zygaena. Additionally, regional shifts in suitability have the potential to affect population connectivity, the access to key habitats, and levels of exposure to other anthropogenic pressures, along with the effectiveness of conservation and management efforts. Our results showcase the importance of climate change for species’ extinction risk assessment and the urgency of its consideration for the design and implementation of conservation measures tailored to the oceans of tomorrow.

3591: While spatial distribution shifts have been documented in many marine fishes under global change, the responses of elasmobranchs have rarely been studied, despite their irreplaceable role in the ecosystems and their high extinction risk, which may have led to an underestimation of their potential additional threats. We used a 24-year-long time series (1997-2020) of scientific bottom trawl surveys to examine the effects of climate change on the spatial distribution of nine elasmobranch species within Northeast Atlantic waters. We found that suitable habitats for four species increased on average by a factor of 1.6 and, for six species, shifted northwestwards and/or in depth over the past two decades. By integrating species traits, we showed changes in habitat suitability led to changes in the elasmobranchs trait-composition. Moreover, communities deepened and their mean trophic level decreased. We also note an increase in the mean community size at maturity correlated in a less pronounced way to a decrease in fecundity. Because skates and sharks are functionally unique and dangerously vulnerable to both climate change and fishing, we advocate for urgent considerations of species traits in management measures because of their utility to better identify species whose loss could have irreversible impacts in face of the myriad of upcoming threats, especially for unmonitored species. In this way, we would gain efficiency in implementing biodiversity conservation.

3592: Climate change is affecting the oceans in different ways. Marine heat waves, for example, are becoming more frequent, more prolonged, and more intense, endangering marine life. Assessing the impact of these extreme events on disease outbreak and dynamics in sharks is poorly understood. Here, we investigated the effects of a simulated (moderate) marine heat wave (MHW; Δ2°C; 9 days) on the physiological (ventilation rates) and biochemical (several oxidative-stress biomarkers on gills, muscle, brain, and liver tissues) condition of juvenile small-spotted catshark (Scyliorhinus canicula) infected with ectoparasite Amyloodinium ocellatum. No mortality differences were observed, but a significant increase in ventilation rates were observed under the MHW treatment. Significant changes in enzymatic antioxidant activities were observed among tissues, but only superoxide dismutase activity was affected under MHW conditions. Protein repair and removal mechanisms (heat shock protein and total ubiquitin), and oxidative damage on lipids (malondialdehyde) and DNA (8-hydroxy-2′- deoxyguanosine) also did not significantly change between treatments. Our result is consistent with other studies that have shown that sharks display some level of resilience to the effects of climate change-related stressors. However, another category of marine heat wave (IV or V for example) could produce other physiological effects.

3593: The role of recreational angling as both a threat to shark stocks and an opportunity to support shark conservation tends to be overlooked. Sharks have been described as the aquatic ‘big game’ equivalent, displayed as ‘trophies’ and caught for the ‘thrill of the fight’. Historical fears of sharks have led to an increase in shark fishing tournaments, increasing the rate of decline of shark populations threatened with extinction. However, modern-day social science studies in the United States and Australia have contradicted these fears, with a growing desire amongst anglers to become advocates for shark conservation. Here, we examine anglers’ motivations behind shark fishing in the United Kingdom (UK) a popular but understudied location for recreational shark fishing. Angler demographics, perceptions towards sharks and perceptions of shark population trends were also explored. A total of seven shark fishing operators and 44 recreational anglers responded to our structured surveys throughout Aug-Nov 2021. Respondents primarily comprised of over-fifty, educated and wealthy male anglers. Anglers were motivated by the ‘appreciation for sharks and nature’ (n=43) and the ‘thrill/challenge’ (n=38). Obtaining a photo (status) was the least popular reason for taking part in shark fishing, further contradicting historical studies. Recreational shark fishing in the UK is strictly catch and release, with anglers demonstrating best practice techniques to minimise stress to caught sharks. We also identify a population of anglers who are knowledgeable about local shark species and recognise their role in contributing to shark conservation but identify a lack of higher-level management to legislate change.

3594: Until relatively recently commercial fisheries have been considered the main driving factor for elasmobranch population declines. However, this belief has begun to shift with the realisation that recreational elasmobranch catches may equal or exceed commercial catches in some regions. Many recreational angling fisheries for elasmobranchs involve high participation in catch-and-release angling practices. However, high release rates may not necessarily equate to high survival rates. Therefore, to assist accurate assessment of the potential impact of recreational angling on elasmobranchs, we attempted to summarise and integrate currently available information on specific risk factors associated with recreational angling, alongside associated mortality rates, as well as information on angler behaviour as it relates to identified risk factors. We categorised the major angling-related effects into two groups: injury-induced effects; and biochemical disruption-induced effects; providing a summary of each group and outlining the main lethal and sub-lethal outcomes stemming from these. These outcomes include post-release mortality, behavioural recovery periods (which may in-turn confer increased predation risks), chronic health impacts, and capture-induced parturition and abortion. Additionally, we detailed a range of angling practices and equipment, including hook-type, hook removal and emersion, as well as inter- and intra-specific factors, including aerobic scope, respiratory mode, body size and species-specific behaviours, which may influence injury and/or mortality rates and should therefore be considered when assessing angling-related impacts. We then utilised these data to provide a range of actionable recommendations for both anglers and policymakers which would serve to reduce the population-level impact of recreational angling on these enigmatic animals.

3595: Recently, analysis of eighteen strandings in eastern Spain has identified fourteen lethal interactions between blue sharks and swordfish. In these cases, the sharks were impaled in the cephalic region by swordfish rostra. While some signs of interaction were easily identifiable, others proved elusive despite thorough physical examinations and dissection on necropsy. Computed Tomography (CT) has emerged as a valuable diagnostic tool for identifying and characterizing these distinctive injuries, even revealing healed wounds from previous impalements. The detailed imagery obtained enables the evaluation of tissue damage and wound trajectory, offering a unique insight into each interaction. We show the efficiency of this technique by using a Somatom Volume Access (Siemens) scanner located at the Oceanogràfic veterinary hospital. Parameters for body exploration included a 5 mm slice thickness and interval, with a retro-recon acquisition of 0.5 mm utilizing lung and mediastinal algorithms. Rostra fragments were discovered embedded in soft tissues or cranial cartilage in twelve sharks, four of which have multiple rostra from past impalements. Two other animals exhibited signs of impalement without fragments. Analysis of the cases always shows adult sharks impaled by juvenile swordfish. The high prevalence (77.8%) and similarity of the interactions diminish the likelihood of chance accidents, suggesting intentional ofensive or defensive behaviour by the swordfish. These data suggest that agonistic interactions between swordfish and blue sharks may be more common than previously thought Due to challenges in lesion detection, impalement may have been overlooked in the past, highlighting the importance of employing CT scans whenever possible.

3596: Fatal interactions between blue sharks (Prionace glauca) and swordfishes (Xiphias gladius) have been described in the western Mediterranean Sea as a cause of stranding and death of the former in the last years. This study describes, both macroscopic and microscopically, the lesions found in eight blue sharks, stranded in Spanish coasts, presenting evidence of impalement from swordfish´s rostrum. All the analysed animals presented the fatal injuries in the head, mainly grouped around the eyes in the frontal plane. Injures were characterized by multiple haemorrhages, predominant heterophilic cell infiltrates, and the presence of fibrin in the fatal injury, which are typical signs of an acute lesion. The most affected tissue was the brain, which showed meningeal and brain haemorrhage, accompanied by encephalitis and encephalomalacia. Additionally, we observed lesions in some eyes that were stabbed, displaying acute panophthalmitis. Furthermore, chronic signs such as the presence of fibroblasts and mononuclear infiltrates in the wounds, as well as rostrums from past interactions completely surrounded by fibrotic connective tissue, were clear indications of past interactions that had healed. These findings suggest that sharks have the potential to survive these types of interactions. The animals showing signs of chronicity exhibited other lesions repeatedly, such as hepatic emaciation, necrotic haemorrhagic ulcers with mononuclear infiltrates in the spiral valve, and enlargement of the renal glomerulus. The complete necropsy and study of the tissues of the stranded sharks proved to be a useful tool to better understand the nature and the consequences of the interaction between these two species.

3597: Baited Remote Underwater Video Systems (BRUVS) are widely used as a non-destructive electronic tool to investigate the abundance and diversity of fish in marine and freshwater environments. Project SIARC is working with local fishers and their charter vessels to deploy BRUVS off the coast of North Wales to obtain footage that improves our understanding of species, including elasmobranchs present in North Wales and their habitat utilisation. So far, from 90 BRUV deployments, 41 different fish species have been recorded, including five elasmobranchs. This presentation will highlight the key findings from the first year of BRUVS deployment. In parallel, the footage obtained from the BRUVS allows us to make life under the Welsh waters visible to citizen scientists globally. Video footage captured is shared via Instant Wild (an online tool that allows the general public to identify wildlife species from remote camera footage across the world), allowing individuals to identify species, contributing to data collection and increasing awareness of the elasmobranchs present in Welsh waters whilst enhancing inclusivity and access of the natural environment. Project SIARC is a collaboration between the Zoological Society of London, Natural Resources Wales and six partners and made possible thanks to the National Lottery Heritage Fund, Welsh Government’s Nature Networks Fund and On the EDGE Conservation.

3598: Monitoring pelagic highly migratory species is challenging, particularly in regions where weather conditions can be unpredictable and adverse. The blue shark Prionace glauca is no exception, and recent estimates of ~10M individuals fished annually, understanding their distribution and habitat preference is important for area-based management. Blue shark swim-with tourism is increasing across various countries, including the UK, providing both a need to understand the nature of these interactions, and an opportunity to gather novel data on this highly migratory species. UK tour operators reported blue shark interaction data 2021-2023, maxN, swimmer numbers and environmental parameters. Further data were obtained on tidal state, depth, SST, and chlorophyll-a concentration. Chum soak time and maxN were used as response variables to understand the drivers of shark occurrence and relative abundance. Preliminary results show that tidal phase, sea surface temperature and depth are likely to be important factors influencing blue shark occurrence, distribution and relative abundance. This study provides not only a unique insight into the ecology and behaviour of a globally important shark species, but has also created a valuable opportunity for ongoing collaboration between science and industry, and a springboard for long-term data collection and active management of a growing blue economy sector.

3599: Photo identification is a non-invasive method used to distinguish individuals in the wild based on some external visual criterium. As a capture-recapture methodology photo-ID allows to evaluate important ecological parameters such as spatio-temporal preferences, philopatry, abundance up to growth rates estimation. Porbeagle shark has encountered a severe decrease all other its range of distribution and was subject to a fishing regulation by European Council (No 23/2010); since that access to biological information on the species is scarce. DRDH team started in 2021 a free diving protocol to follow hotspots of porbeagle (Lamna nasus) established in the northern cost of Brittany. A data set of videos and photos was gathered through regular standardized dives from DRDH team as well as social media and stakeholder inquiries. We defined 5 different phenotypic marks which allow us to identify more than 100 individual sharks and thus initiate the first and build up a working catalog. Sightings occurred from may to October between 2015 and 2023 with some re sightings confirmed within weeks, months or years distance. All encountered sharks were females, ranging from 1,5 to 3 meters Lt documented for their maturity status. The initial results of this study support the ecological importance of the area for the species in regards to biotic and abiotic parameters. The participatory science dimension of the project offers interesting public awareness possibilities in addition to data provisioning and collaborative tool for other international research teams. Outputs will be discussed in the context of a growing interest for shark and underwater tourism.

3600: Despite the charismatic status of the Mobulidae family, our current understanding of this group remains limited. Given their highly migratory nature and the current global vulnerability they face, it is imperative to gain a comprehensive understanding of their ecology and behaviour in order to support conservation actions. Up until now, there has been a significant knowledge gap in mobulid research in the Canary Islands. Situated in the Eastern Atlantic, the Canary Islands offer unique opportunities for studying these animals. Manta Catalog represents the first line of work focused on the Mobulidae family in the region. Through community science, engaging the fishing and diving sectors, and by reviewing historical sources of information, we have compiled baseline information on the occurrence of this group in the archipelago. This work significantly contributes to our knowledge on these threatened animals in the Canary Islands and emphasises the importance of community science in long-term studies of migratory and pelagic species.

3601: Most elasmobranch populations are under pressure, and to advise policy makers on appropriate conservation measures, data on abundance, life history traits, spawning grounds and population structure are required. The application of DNA based techniques can provide some of this information, but commonly is dependent on tissue sampling (e.g., muscle, scale and blood) which requires handling and potentially underestimate less common species. Environmental DNA (eDNA) is shown as a reliable tool for the assessment of elasmobranch species diversity, but so far is unable to provide reliable data on population diversity. Egg cases of oviparous elasmobranchs can form a valuable aid in determining a species spatial distribution, defining spawning areas and DNA based analysis of population structure. So far, egg cases for this type of research were collected from both commercial fisheries and scientific surveys, generally with the embryo still inside, ensuring the quality of DNA. However, many of the egg cases wash up on shore after hatching departure or predation. When exposed to the elements, the genetic material in the egg case will start degrading, but DNA fragments of sufficient quality could still be viable for population genetics. We now present the successful isolation and sequencing of 2kb long mtDNA fragments from 14-day-old, hatched egg cases using a combination of liquid nitrogen, keratinase and collagenase. Developing this method further, beached egg cases collected by means of citizen science can provide a useful tool to determine oviparous elasmobranch population structure with limited resources and the added bonus of creating public awareness.

3602: Deep-sea chondrichthyans have been underestimated and overshadowed. This misconception assumes they are unaffected by global changes and face minimal fishing threats. Among chondrichthyans, the order Chimaeriformes, specifically the rabbitfish Chimaera monstrosa, is one of the most striking examples. Our three-year research focused on unravelling the mysteries surrounding C. monstrosa in the Northeast Atlantic, where it is commonly caught as bycatch. It is classified as 'Near Threatened' by IUCN in European waters. Although we documented its abundance, habitat preferences, and responses to warming waters, significant gaps persist in understanding its life history traits and ecology, hindering targeted conservation measures. Using models and mapping tools, our study aimed to identify diverse populations and critical areas in need of protection. Along the Norwegian coast, we observed variations in growth rates and maturity, indicating potential adaptations to fisheries or environmental conditions. We located some areas that could arguably function as mating or nursery areas. Our research suggests that the newly colonized waters of northern Norway host a well-developed population of C. monstrosa. This colonization and potential further expansion northward, driven by warmer waters, underscore the necessity for monitoring critical areas, vulnerability to warming waters, and potential changes in the food web, particularly in the warming and heavily impacted North Sea. By providing insights into C. monstrosa's distribution patterns, regional variations, and implications for conservation, these findings contribute to the development of species-specific conservation measures.
3603: High bycatch of elasmobranchs and their decline in the Adriatic Sea call for management actions. Within the Italian monitoring programs of the Marine Strategy Framework Directive, we investigated the post-release survival rates of juveniles of commercial species to explore the efficacy and feasibility of the implementation of a minimum conservation reference size (MCRS). From May 2020 to June 2023, through 90 on-board fishing trips using different fishing gears we evaluated the At-Vessel Mortality (AVM; 3443 individuals, 14 species), Short-term post-release mortality (St-PRM; two hours after capture, on board, 788 individuals, 14 species) and Long-term PRM (Lt-PRM; 72 hours after capture, at laboratory, 121 individuals, 3 species). AMV was on average 16%, varying among species, fishing gears and seasons and depending on factors such as temperature and duration of air exposure. St-PRM and Lt-PRM were generally low, below 16% and 20%, respectively. To better estimate mortality, by combining conventional tagging and acoustic telemetry, in the framework of the MedBycatch project, we investigated Lt-PRM in the field. We tagged 1816 individuals of 16 species with spaghetti tags, 61 individuals of 3 species with acoustic tags. The tagging study contributed also to the understanding of the use of space and to highlight residency and site fidelity behaviours. To rigorously explore the potential efficacy and sustainability of the release of juveniles, we constructed individual based population dynamics models to assess the expected recovery of populations according to different MCRS and survival rates.

3604: The poor conservation status of Chondrichthyes in the Mediterranean Sea requires effective management strategies. Ad-hoc conservation measures for different areas and species are needed. In this perspective, the By ElasmoCatch Project is focusing on the Amvrakikos Gulf (Greece). Here, only small-scale fishery is operating, using set-nets and longlines, in some cases targeting Mustelus mustelus and Myliobatidae. From 2022 until now, 547 fishing operations have been monitored through interviews (532) and onboard surveys (45). A total of 1176 elasmobranchs have been recorded. Among the 10 species present, 2 Critically Endangered (Mediterranean Region) stingrays Aetomylaeus bovinus and Gymnura altavela were commonly caught (25.5% of recorded elasmobranchs). Moreover, identification issues for specimens of the family Dasyatidae emerged. To better understand the biology and ecology of elasmobranchs in the area and clearly identify the species, a multidisciplinary approach is used (e.g., data on life-history traits, stomach contents, genetic). Finally, we are investigating post-release mortality (through 40 minutes tank maintenance, 92; and a conventional-tagging program, 189) to understand the efficacy of release as a management strategy. Given the high biodiversity and presence of both pregnant females and newborns of different species, this region appears to be crucial for elasmobranchs, and it was proposed as Important Shark and Ray Area (ISRA). Future steps will include an acoustic-tagging program to further understand survival after capture and use of space, heavy-metal analyses, and testing of other mitigation measures (e.g., gear modifications), with the final aim to find the best management strategy and its implementation by the local community.

3605: Commonly, there is a shortage of available omics resources from elasmobranchs on public databases, such as genomes, transcriptomes, and mitogenomes. This highlights the importance of taking the most advantage of available resources. Thus, we assessed the potential of using transcriptomes from elasmobranchs to computationally recover their mitogenomes. Within this work, we gathered more than 30 transcriptomic entries from the NCBI Database from elasmobranch species whose mitogenome was not available. We were able to perform mitochondrial genome assemblies for 10 species whose mitogenome was previously unreported: Isistius brasiliensis, Negaprion brevirostris, Potamotrygon amandae, P. leopoldi, Rhizoprionodon taylori, R. terraenovae, Scyliorhinus rotifer, Squalus suckleyi, Tetronarce californica, and Urobatis jamaicensis. The recovered assemblies ranged from 16,620 to 17,710 nucleotides, and half of the final assemblies presented a 100% recovery rate (the lowest reached 92%). The assembly of these mitogenomes will empower further studies that can be relevant to understanding the evolutionary and ecological framework of elasmobranchs, especially considering the important role of the mitochondrial genes on oxidative phosphorylation. Additionally, it will assist population genomic studies that often rely on partial mitochondrial genomes, extending the already powerful tool of transcriptomics.

3606: Recreational shark fishing accounts for millions of shark captures each year across the world, with many fishers now employing a "catch and release" (C&R) approach. In Europe, C&R fisheries for sharks are widespread and involve thousands of sharks each year, including the blue shark (Prionace glauca) and the porbeagle shark (Lamna nasus). Despite this, studies on the potential impacts of C&R fishing are generally lacking, with only one investigation conducted on porbeagle sharks in North America and none on blue sharks globally. To address the potential impacts of a range of handling and environmental conditions, this ongoing study uses short-term electronic tags (45 days) to assess the effects of C&R fishing on the behaviour and mortality of blue and porbeagle sharks caught recreationally in southwest UK waters and the northern Adriatic Sea. To date, no mortalities have been observed among tagged sharks (n=18). However, high-resolution data obtained from retrieved tags (n=5) suggests differences in diving patterns between the immediate post-release period and later stages of tracking, indicating a potential behavioural impact of capture. These preliminary results suggest that, within the range of handling and environmental conditions studied so far, C&R fishing for blue and porbeagle sharks is unlikely to results in mortality with 45 days of release, although sublethal short-term effects on animal welfare may require further attention. Further research is necessary to examine the short- and long-term behavioural effects of C&R fishing and identify specific aspects of the practice that may be refined to improve outcomes for sharks.

3607: The survival of chondrichthyans is a major marine conservation concern, with over one-third of species currently at risk of extinction due to their exceptional vulnerability and low resilience to high levels of exploitation. However, our extremely limited knowledge of their basic ecology hampers the implementation of proper management and conservation actions. There is also a knowledge gap on the genetic diversity and population structure of these species at different spatial scales. This is especially true for migratory species, such as the Sicklefin devil ray (Mobula tarapacana), that utilizes the restricted coastal habitats of oceanic islands. Understanding the degree of genetic connectivity allows to define population boundaries and infer dispersal patterns, while describing genetic diversity will allow to inform appropriate measures to preserve it. To fill this knowledge gap, we used a genetic multi-marker approach. We evaluated population structure and assessed connectivity at different spatial scales – from ocean basins to the island groups within the Azores archipelago - through the analysis of Single Nucleotide Polymorphism (SNP) markers and Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA). The results of this project will provide science-based knowledge to support suitable management and conservation actions, regionally and globally.

3608: To achieve sustainable shark fisheries, it is as important to understand the social and economic drivers of overfishing as it is the biological drivers and environmental consequences. The extinction risk of sharks is disproportionately higher in coastal tropical waters where small-scale fisheries dominate, presenting unique management challenges. Small-scale fisheries provide a critical source of economic and nutritional security, but fishers are among the most vulnerable socio-economic groups because their exposure to economic, social, and environmental shocks is combined with limited adaptive capacity. Using Kenya and Zanzibar as a case study, we examine the interactions between sharks and small-scale fisheries. We find that sharks are an important source of economic and nutritional security, primarily from species threatened with extinction. Further, the most economically valuable sharks are larger, slower reproducing, and more likely to be threatened with extinction, providing a strong economic incentive to target endangered species. Given the high economic motivation and intensive fishing pressure, small-scale fisheries are undoubtedly important contributors to the ongoing decline of many threatened shark species. The decline of sharks may have damaging consequences for wider marine ecosystems and ecosystem services. In the absence of effective fisheries management, we show that within small-scale fisheries the conditions exist for an economically incentivised positive feedback loop in which vulnerable fishers are driven to persistently overfish vulnerable and declining resources. In doing so, they undermine their own economic and nutritional security and that of their communities. To be successful management must break the feedback loop or be doomed to failure.

3609: Against a context of global change, the world is facing new challenges. This is the backdrop to our project to build an eco-responsible research vessel called the Parsifal. For over 2 years, the members of our team have been renovating this boat with the aim of making it an ambassador for sharks. The ultimate goal is to navigate all around the world using La Pérouse's route, while carrying out a range of scientific studies. This boat will enable us to carry out a wide range of projects on sharks in remote areas, focusing on conservation issues, studies and surveys in isolated areas for example. Shark diving, water sampling and fisheries data collection will all be part of the programme. Our expeditions will be accompanied by scientific documentaries to show the reality of shark science to people who are not involved in this field, thus highlighting the different players at sea. The aim of this eco-responsible vessel is to play an active role in the study and conservation of sharks around the world. Various scientists from all around the world, studying different aspects of sharks, will be presented and they will be invited to collaborate with our work to carry out expeditions and take samples throughout the expeditions.
3610: The Nursehound Scyliorhinus stellaris (Linnaeus, 1758) is a medium-sized catshark that resides in the Northeast Atlantic and Mediterranean Sea. It is classified as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species (Near Threatened under the European and Mediterranean assessments) and although distribution is patchy, they can be locally abundant. This oviparous species occurs on the continental and insular shelf, generally inhabiting shallow coastal waters where they have been documented depositing their eggs. The curled tendrils extending from the capsule are used to anchor the eggcase to a substrate while the embryo develops over an incubation period of approximately 9 – 11 months. A sheltered channel was discovered in south Devon (southwest England) where Nursehounds were consistently depositing their eggs, usually attached to the algae Rainbow Wrack Ericaria selaginoides (Linnaeus) Molinari & Guiry, 2020. Accessible by snorkelling on a low spring tide, this site has been visited on a regular basis (once to twice a month) since April 2014 to monitor developing eggcases, assess the level of biofouling, and document freshly deposited eggcases. To date, 326 eggcases have been recorded at this site (average 36 per year), with 159 having been seen consistently from deposition through to hatching, others have been predated upon or have washed away during storms. The goal of this citizen science project is to determine the average development period in order to gain further insight on the species in the wild and gain a greater understanding of egg deposition in this species.
3611: The Great Eggcase Hunt is a citizen science initiative that was established by the Shark Trust in 2003. Over the last 20 years, the project has received ~25,000 submissions from ~13,000 participants, (although this figure represents far greater pool of participants from group events) totalling over 440,000 eggcases from 46 oviparous elasmobranch species around the world. Although the majority of data is from the British Isles, where the project was established, the Great Eggcase Hunt receives submissions from around the world. Multiple identification guides have been created in collaboration with regional organisations (i.e. Turkey, Portugal and Australia), along with development of a citizen science mobile app. Analysis of this dataset can be used to pick out temporal and seasonal patterns: It can allow hotpots for eggcases to be identified – signifying potential egglaying grounds - as well as highlighting locations that are lacking in records and may require more searching effort. Data submitted from regular reporters allow for a finer scale understanding of seasonality of eggcase finds, with regular reporters spread across the UK allowing comparison. Data from the Great Eggcase Hunt has led to an improved understanding of eggcase morphology (e.g., the Common Skate complex) and can even be used to help identify possible spawning grounds. As well as species-specific data, a dataset of this size provides a valuable insight into citizen science engagement, including the growth of the project in terms of both numbers (of participants and eggcase finds) and spread of engagement, along with the seasonality of reporting.
3612: The global shark trade plays a major role in the exploitation of shark populations. Multiple studies have uncovered fraud in European shark meat markets, including sales of prohibited and threatened species, and high levels of mislabelling. However, to date, few have assessed large-scale patterns across multiple countries. Combining samples collected by citizen science projects and NGOs with data from a systematic meta-analysis, this study investigated a total of 792 shark products identified using DNA barcoding, across ten countries: Greece, Italy, UK, Spain, France, Germany, the Netherlands, Portugal, Austria and Iceland; and four retailer types: fish markets, fishmongers, processed products and supermarkets. The blue shark (Prionace glauca), listed as critically endangered in the Mediterranean, was the most identified species in the study, especially among Mediterranean countries. Furthermore, the results indicate significant differences in species utilisation across countries, potentially influenced by geographic proximity to different fisheries. Worryingly, vulnerable species were found on sale in all countries and retailer types in the study. Mislabelling rates were relatively high (32.4%), potentially driven by the opportunistic use of threatened species from bycatch. Overall, the study highlights the need for improved implementation of management and labelling legislation to enable more informed consumer choices and to reduce the overexploitation of shark populations.

3613: In the Mediterranean Sea, more than 40% of the assessed chondrichthyan species are considered threatened. In addition, there are two other complexity factors that make the conservation challenge more difficult and increase the risk of extinction of cartilaginous fishes: 1) elasmobranchs pass through multiple jurisdictions with different fishery and environmental regulations; 2) sharks and their relatives also have different social and economic considerations, serving in some cases as subsistence for communities. In this controversial scenario, where common environmental policy actions are really difficult, marine stakeholders can play a key role to start a concrete conservation of marine biodiversity, especially for organisms still considered dangerous, like sharks and their relatives. The LIFE ELIFE project (LIFE18 NAT/IT/000846), co-funded by the EU LIFE programme, includes two conservation actions focused on the awareness and the engagememt of citizens and stakeholders, in order to increase their attention on the great vulnerability of these animals. In this framework, here we report four recent best practice events for the conservation of elasmobranchs, carried out by common citizens and professional fishers, allowing the survival of 2 manta rays (Mobula mobular), one blue shark (Prionace glauca) and one angel shark (Squatina sp.). The success of these initiatives was based on the strong voluntary collaboration among several actors (citizens, scientists, fishers, authorities, MPAs) and it highlights how their engagement can be the real key tool to carry out concrete actions aimed to elasmobranch conservation in the Mediterranean Sea, anticipating common political steps.

3614: Many species of elasmobranchs are overfished, and populations have declined substantially, both internationally and within UK waters, including in Sussex. Research indicates that the majority of elasmobranchs landed in trawl fisheries in the English Channel are below their L50, and therefore likely before they have reproduced. This suggests size-based management, which aims to increase the proportion of individuals that are harvested post-reproductive age therefore increasing recruitment and population growth, is appropriate in Sussex. The conservation challenges faced by elasmobranchs include their tendency to be caught as bycatch, however commercial fishers are constrained by quota restrictions on skate and ray species (certain species are aggregated into a single term 'Skates and Rays). Recreational fishers are not always subject to the same restrictions as commercial fishers and are more likely to be receptive to voluntary measures. Therefore, to promote sustainable fishing practices amongst local anglers, Sussex Inshore Fisheries and Conservation Authority (IFCA) developed a voluntary code of conduct that details recommended minimum landing sizes, a welfare guide, and a concise location-specific ID guide. It is also intended to help commercial fishers engage in more conservation-orientated behaviours regarding how elasmobranch bycatch is processed. Minimum sizes were selected based on a literature review used to calculate the average size at which 50% of the population has reached sexual maturity (L50), and the most threatened and least protected species were considered priorities for inclusion in the code of conduct. Sussex IFCA plan to publish this code of conduct alongside confirmation of broader sized based management within the district.

3615: Recreational fisheries in the Northern Adriatic Sea consist of a range of fishing techniques targeting several species (Pranovi et al., 2016). Drifting is one of the most commnly used methods, employed especially for catch and release (C&R) fishing of Atlantic bluefin tuna (Thunnus thynnus). The fishery is also known to accidentally catch pelagic shark species, though the species composition, seasonality, and potential impact of the fishery on the shark assemblage in the region is poorly understood. In the last four years, logbook data was collected in collaboration with nearly 20 drifting fishers to assess the by-catch rate and area of occurrence of three neritic sharks. Among these species, the blue shark (Prionace glauca) is the most frequently caught, followed by the common thresher shark (Alopias vulpinus) and the sandbar shark (Carcharhinus plumbeus). Questionnaires were also used to gather local ecological knowledge (LEK) regarding the by-catch rate, area of seasonal occurrence, age composition, and post-release survival perception for the three species. Finally, post-release survival of these species is being assessed through the deployment of a combination of conventional (spaghetti tag), acoustic (sentinel array of 18 VR2tX receivers and V13 transmitters by Innovasea) and satellite (sPAT) tagging. This multidisciplinary approach has the potential to contribute to closing the knowledge gap on the movement ecology of these species in the Northern Adriatic Sea, while also helping to quantify the potential impact of drifting fishing on shark populations.
